source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. IV (Montreuil)

1.title: De persona, tempore et origine sancti Job; et quis sit auctor libri hujus.
1.title_en: On the person, the time and the origin of holy Job; and who is the author of this book

paras.t: De persona et tempore atque origine sancti Job, quantum ad multa, non videtur magna certitudo faciliter posse haberi, præsertim quum sancti catholicique doctores inde variis modis inveniantur locuti. Primo igitur perscrutandum, quis fuerit iste Job, et de ejus origine. Itaque Augustinus, Ambrosius, Gregorius, et multi expositores sequentes Doctores illos præcipuos, concorditer dicunt, quod fuit natione Idumæus, de semine Esau natus. Dicit enim Augustinus super illud Genesis, Mortuus est autem Balac, et regnavit pro eo Jobab filius Zaræ de Bosra. Quod autem per hunc Jobab S. Gregorius intelligat Job, apertissime constat ex his, quæ primo Moralium super Job scribit statim post prologum. Ambrosius quoque super epistolam ad Romanos idem insinuat. Albertus etiam hic scribit, quod ante fuit ei nomen Jobab, eratque filius cujusdam Zaræ, qui fuit filius filii Esau, de quadam matre nomine Bosra natus, ita quod quintus fuit ab Esau, vel quartus secundum alium modum; sextus autem aut septimus ab Abraham. Et dicitur rex fuisse terræ illius, et rex secundus: nam ante eum regnavit Balac; post eum regnavit Husam. Hucusque Albertus.
paras.en: Concerning the person, the time and the origin of holy Job, it seems that on many points no great certainty can easily be had, especially since the holy catholic doctors are found to have spoken of it in various ways. First, then, we must search out who this Job was, and his origin. Augustine, Ambrose, Gregory, and many expositors who follow those chief Doctors, say with one accord that he was an Idumean by nation, born of the seed of Esau. For Augustine says so on that text of Genesis: [[Gen 36:33|And Bela died, and Jobab, the son of Zara, of Bosra, reigned in his stead|Mortuus est autem Balac, et regnavit pro eo Jobab filius Zaræ de Bosra]] [Denis's text reads *Balac* for *Bela*; the edition marks the name and gives *Bela* in the margin]. That by this Jobab St. Gregory understands Job is quite plain from what he writes in the first book of the Morals on Job, straight after the prologue. Ambrose too hints the same, on the Epistle to the Romans. Albert also writes here that his name before was Jobab, and that he was the son of one Zara, who was the son of a son of Esau, and was born of a mother named Bosra; so that he was the fifth from Esau, or the fourth by another reckoning, and the sixth or seventh from Abraham. And he is said to have been king of that land, and its second king: for before him Balac reigned, and after him Husam. Thus far Albert.

paras.t: Porro de hac materia plenius loquitur Augustinus octavodecimo de Civitate Dei, capitulo 47, dicens: Nec ipsos Judæos existimo audere contendere, id est contentiose asserere, neminem pertinuisse ad Deum præter Israelitas, ex quo, id est ab eo tempore, quo propago Israel, id est generatio Jacob seu procreatio filiorum ejus, esse cœpit. Populus enim revera, qui proprie Dei populus diceretur, nullus alius fuit, videlicet quam Israelitæ. Homines autem quosdam non terrena, sed cœlesti societate ad veros Israelitas supernæ cives patriæ pertinentes, etiam in aliis gentibus fuisse, negare non possunt. Quod si negent, facile convincuntur de sancto et mirabili viro Job, qui nec indigena, id est inde natus, puta ex Jacob seu Israel, nec proselytus, id est advena, populi Israel fuit; sed ex gente Idumæa genus ducens, ibi ortus, ibi et mortuus est.
paras.en: Augustine speaks of this matter more fully in the eighteenth book of the City of God, chapter 47, saying: Nor do I think that the Jews themselves dare to contend (that is, to maintain contentiously) that no one has belonged to God except the Israelites, since (that is, from the time when) the offspring of Israel (that is, the generation of Jacob, or the begetting of his sons) began to be. For in truth there was no other people that was properly called the people of God, namely, than the Israelites[[Lev 20:26||]][[Deut 7:6||]][[Deut 14:2||]][[Deut 26:18||]] [the margin also gives a reference in Numbers whose numerals cannot be read in the scan]. But they cannot deny that there have been, in other nations too, certain men who belonged, not by an earthly but by a heavenly fellowship, to the true Israelites, the citizens of the country above. And if they deny it, they are easily refuted by the holy and wonderful man Job, who was neither a native (that is, one born of it, as from Jacob or Israel) nor a proselyte (that is, a newcomer) of the people of Israel; but, drawing his descent from the nation of Idumea, he was born there and there he died.

paras.t: Sed de hac re beatus Hieronymus aliter sentit, libro de Hebraicis quæstionibus super Genesim, dicens, quod Job descendit de Nachor fratre Abrahæ. Legitur quippe in Genesi, quod Melcha genuit viro suo, videlicet Nachor, octo filios, quorum primus vocatus est Hus, secundus Buz. Dicit ergo Hieronymus, quod Job ortus sit de Nachor per primogenitum ejus nomine Hus, a quo terra illa dicitur Hus nominata, ita quod Hus est nomen viri et terræ. Unde in principio hujus voluminis scriptum est: Vir erat in terra Hus, nomine Job. Præterea, de secundo filio Nachor, id est de ipso Buz, dicit Hieronymus descendisse ipsum Eliu, de quo infra fit mentio, qui cognominatur Buzites, tanquam de tribu Buz. Idem quoque dicunt Hebræi, quos Hieronymus in hac assertione secutus est. Sed et in Scholastica historia idem asseritur, cujus conscriptor etiam aperte testatur eos errare, qui dicunt ipsum Job de Esau descendisse. Unde posterioribus quibusdam videtur magis credendum Hieronymo et Hebræis, tanquam in talibus historiis ac genealogiis amplius certis.
paras.en: But blessed Jerome thinks otherwise on this matter, in the book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis, saying that Job descended from Nachor, the brother of Abraham. For we read in Genesis that Melcha bore to her husband, that is, to Nachor, eight sons[[Gen 22:20||]], of whom the first was called Hus, the second Buz[[Gen 22:21||]]. Jerome says, then, that Job sprang from Nachor through his firstborn, named Hus, after whom that land is said to have been named Hus; so that Hus is the name both of the man and of the land. Hence at the beginning of this book it is written: [[1:1|There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job|Vir erat in terra Hus, nomine Job]]. Moreover, Jerome says that from Nachor's second son, that is, from Buz himself, there descended that Eliu who is mentioned below and is surnamed the Buzite[[Job 32:6||]], as being of the tribe of Buz. The Hebrews too say the same, and Jerome followed them in this assertion. And the Scholastic History [the *Historia scholastica* of Peter Comestor] asserts the same, and its author even testifies openly that those err who say that Job descended from Esau. Hence it seems to certain later writers that Jerome and the Hebrews are rather to be believed, as being more sure in such histories and genealogies.

paras.t: Quidam etiam imaginantur Augustinum atque Ambrosium motos ad præfatam positionem ex similitudine nominum horum, Job et Jobab. Verumtamen hoc non reor; nec aliquis Doctorum istorum sublimium tangit istud motivum: nam debile esset. Sed potius arbitror motos eos ex translatione Septuaginta interpretum tunc famosa, qui habet, Vir fuit in terra Ausitide: quæ terra fertur fuisse in finibus Idumææ atque Arabiæ. Quod autem Septuaginta ita transtulerunt, testatur quodam loco Hieronymus. Insuper in aliquibus bibliis, in fine libri Job, vel in fine secundi prologi Hieronymi super Job, additur: Fertur autem Job in terra habitasse Ausitide, et erat ei ante nomen Jobab, et erat quartus ab Esau, etc. Sed istud non est in Hebræo secundum Hieronymum; nec sunt verba Hieronymi, sed alicujus forsan expositoris.
paras.en: Some also imagine that Augustine and Ambrose were moved to the position mentioned above by the likeness of these names, Job and Jobab. But I do not think so; nor does any of those lofty Doctors touch on that motive: for it would be a weak one. Rather I judge that they were moved by the translation of the Seventy interpreters, famous at that time, which has: There was a man in the land of Ausitis [the Septuagint's rendering of v. 1, where the Vulgate has *in terra Hus*]: and that land is said to have been on the borders of Idumea and Arabia. That the Seventy translated so, Jerome testifies in a certain place. Besides, in some Bibles, at the end of the book of Job, or at the end of Jerome's second prologue on Job, there is added: Now Job is said to have dwelt in the land of Ausitis, and his name before was Jobab, and he was the fourth from Esau, etc. But according to Jerome this is not in the Hebrew; nor are these the words of Jerome, but perhaps of some expositor.

paras.t: Nunc inquirendum, quo tempore fuerit sanctus Job. Circa quod scribit S. Augustinus octavodecimo de Civitate Dei, capitulo 47: Cujus (scilicet Job) tempora quamvis non inveniamus in chronicis, colligimus tamen ex libro ejus, quem pro suo merito Israelitæ in auctoritatem canonicam receperunt, tertia generatione posteriorem fuisse quam Israel, id est Jacob patriarcham, fratrem Esau. Ex quo videtur, quod secundum Augustinum Job fuit tertius seu quartus post Esau. Unde aliqui dicunt, quod fuit pronepos ejus, asserentes quod fuit filius Balac, filii Beor, filii Esau. Quibus obviare videtur, quod nec in Genesi, nec primo Paralipomenon, in quibus locis describitur generatio Esau, nec alibi in Scripturis legitur Beor fuisse immediatus filius Esau. Tamen primo Paralipomenon habetur, quod Bale, post quem regnavit Jobab, fuit filius Beor. Qui autem primo Paralipomenon Bale vocatur, in Genesi dicitur Balac, secundum expositores. Rursus prædictum est, quod Jobab fuit filius Zaræ.
paras.en: Now we must inquire at what time holy Job lived. On this St. Augustine writes in the eighteenth book of the City of God, chapter 47: Though we do not find his times (that is, Job's) in the chronicles, yet we gather from his book, which the Israelites for its merit received into canonical authority, that he came three generations after Israel, that is, after the patriarch Jacob, the brother of Esau. From this it seems that according to Augustine Job was the third or fourth after Esau. Hence some say that he was his great-grandson, asserting that he was the son of Balac, the son of Beor, the son of Esau. Against these it seems to tell that neither in Genesis[[Gen 36:1||]] nor in the first book of Paralipomenon[[1 Par 1:35||]], the places where the generation of Esau is described, nor anywhere else in the Scriptures, do we read that Beor was Esau's immediate son. Yet in the first of Paralipomenon we have it that Bale, after whom Jobab reigned, was the son of Beor[[1 Par 1:43||]][[1 Par 1:44||]]. And he who in the first of Paralipomenon is called Bale is called Balac in Genesis, according to the expositors. Again, it was said above that Jobab was the son of Zara.

paras.t: Præterea, juxta prædicta sequi videtur, quod Job ante Moysen fuerit: quod et multi concedunt. Sed Gregorius, quem Glossa sequitur, contradicit, asserens sanctum Job fuisse tempore judicum populi Israel. Argumentum autem Gregorii est, quoniam in Genesi inter reges qui in Idumæa regnaverunt, antequam filii Israel regem habuerunt, Jobab annumeratur. Ex quo patet quod Gregorius præsupponit, per Jobab intelligi Job, et per tempus præcedens præsidentiam regum Israel, intelligi judicum tempus. Vult quoque Gregorius, quod Moyses spiritu prophetico loquebatur de dominio Jobab posterioris Moyse, secundum hanc positionem. Dicit enim Gregorius: Quia in libro Geneseos Jobab de stirpe Esau descendisse, et Balac filio Beor in regnum successisse describitur; hunc beatum Job longe ante Moysis tempora exstitisse crediderunt, morem profecto sacri eloquii nescientes: quia in superioribus suis partibus solet breviter longe post secutura perstringere, quum studet ad alia subtilius enumeranda properare. Unde et illic Jobab, priusquam reges in Israel exsisterent, fuisse describitur. Nequaquam ergo exstitisse ante legem cognoscitur, qui Israeliticorum judicum tempore fuisse memoratur. Verumtamen argumentum istud non cogit. Quidam enim (ut etiam in Scholastica historia continetur) dicunt Moysen non describere reges Idumææ, nisi usque ad illum quem tempore suo ultimum cognoscere potuit. Per tempus quoque præcedens reges Israel, quorum primus exstitit Saul, non est necesse præcise intelligere tempus judicum, sed intelligi potest omne tempus duodecim tribuum usque ad Saul. Denique ista determinatio temporis Job, procedit secundum eos qui dicunt eum de Esau descendisse, secundum modum præfatum.
paras.en: Further, from what has been said it seems to follow that Job lived before Moses: and many grant this. But Gregory, whom the Gloss follows, contradicts it, asserting that holy Job lived in the time of the judges of the people of Israel. Gregory's argument is that in Genesis, among the kings who reigned in Idumea before the children of Israel had a king[[Gen 36:31||]], Jobab is reckoned[[Gen 36:33||]]. From this it is plain that Gregory presupposes that by Jobab Job is meant, and by the time before the rule of the kings of Israel, the time of the judges. Gregory holds too that Moses was speaking in the spirit of prophecy of the dominion of Jobab, who on this position came after Moses. For Gregory says: Because in the book of Genesis Jobab is described as descended from the stock of Esau and as having succeeded Balac the son of Beor in the kingdom[[Gen 36:33||]], they believed that this blessed Job lived long before the times of Moses, being plainly ignorant of the manner of sacred speech, which in its earlier parts is wont to touch briefly on things that follow long after, when it is eager to hasten on to recount other things more minutely. Hence there too Jobab is described as having lived before there were kings in Israel. By no means, then, is he known to have lived before the Law, who is recorded to have lived in the time of the judges of the Israelites. But that argument does not compel. For some (as is contained also in the Scholastic History) say that Moses describes the kings of Idumea only up to the one whom he could know as the last in his own time. Nor, by the time before the kings of Israel, of whom Saul was the first[[1 Kings 10:1||]][[1 Kings 11:15||]], need we understand precisely the time of the judges; it can be understood as the whole time of the twelve tribes up to Saul. Lastly, this fixing of Job's time goes by those who say that he descended from Esau, in the way described above.

paras.t: Sed quia positio S. Hieronymi præinducta, multis probabilior apparet, scrutandum quo tempore sanctus Job secundum hanc fuerit viam. Sicut autem Hieronymus et Scholastica historia cum Hebræis dicunt Job descendisse de Nachor per Hus, et Eliu Buziten de eodem per Buz; sic dicunt Eliu istum, esse illum qui in libro Numerorum Balaam nuncupatur, quem Balac rex advocavit. Quo dato, sequetur quod Job et Moyses contemporanei fuerint. Eliu enim disputavit cum Job, et idem Eliu seu Balaam circa finem vitæ Moysis fuit occisus a filiis Israel ante Moysis obitum, ut patet in Numeris. Constat etiam ex infra scriptis, quod Eliu quando contra Job disputavit, satis juvenis fuit. Quot vero post hoc fluxerint anni ante interfectionem ipsius, non constat; et si non multi anni illi fuisse putentur, posset fortasse positio ista cum Gregorio aliqualiter concordari. Job namque post disputationem curationemque suam vixit annis centum et quadraginta, ut infra patet. Post mortem vero Moysis usque ad judiciariam præsidentiam Othoniel primi judicis Israel, forte pauciores anni fuerunt. Othoniel enim tempore Moysis fuit, et filiam Caleb duxit uxorem statim post ingressum filiorum Israel in terram promissionis. Imo, quia Job ante suam percussionem provectæ fuit ætatis, potuit fieri ut et tempore Moysis fuerit, et tempore alicujus judicum Israel.
paras.en: But since St. Jerome's position, brought forward above, appears more probable to many, we must search out at what time holy Job lived by this way. Now as Jerome and the Scholastic History, with the Hebrews, say that Job descended from Nachor through Hus, and Eliu the Buzite from the same through Buz, so they say that this Eliu is the one who in the book of Numbers is called Balaam, whom king Balac called for[[Num 22:5||]]. Granting this, it will follow that Job and Moses were contemporaries. For Eliu disputed with Job[[Job 32:1||]], and the same Eliu or Balaam was slain by the children of Israel near the end of Moses' life, before Moses' death, as is plain in Numbers[[Num 31:8||]]. It is clear also from what is written below that Eliu, when he disputed against Job, was quite young[[Job 32:6||]]. How many years passed after this before he was slain is not clear; and if they are thought not to have been many, this position might perhaps be brought into some agreement with Gregory. For Job, after his disputation and his healing, lived a hundred and forty years, as is plain below[[Job 42:16||]]. And from the death of Moses to the judgeship of Othoniel, the first judge of Israel, there were perhaps rather few years. For Othoniel was alive in the time of Moses, and took Caleb's daughter to wife straight after the children of Israel entered the land of promise[[Jos 15:17||]]. Indeed, since Job was of advanced age before his affliction, it could be that he lived both in the time of Moses and in the time of one of the judges of Israel.

paras.t: Verumtamen omnibus hinc inde, quorum multa omitto, diligenter pensatis, de hac re nil certum esse opinor, quantum ad temporis determinationem. Unde S. Thomas in prologo expositionis suæ super Job, de prætactis difficultatibus se expediens atque pertransiens, ait: Quo autem tempore fuit Job, vel ex quibus gentibus duxit originem, et an ipse vel alius librum hunc scripserit, non est præsentis intentionis discutere.
paras.en: Yet when everything on either side has been carefully weighed (and I leave much of it out), I think that nothing is certain on this matter, as far as fixing the time is concerned. Hence St. Thomas, in the prologue of his exposition on Job, freeing himself from the difficulties just touched on and passing over them, says: At what time Job lived, or from what nations he drew his origin, and whether he or another wrote this book, it is not our present purpose to discuss.

paras.t: Præterea unum me movet, quia si tempore Moysis fuit, mirum apparet quod Deus de eo perhibuit, quod non fuit ei similis in terra; præsertim quum in Numeris loquens de Moyse ad Aaron et Mariam: Si fuerit, inquit, inter vos Propheta, in visione apparebo ei, vel per somnium loquar ad eum. At non talis servus meus Moyses, qui in omni domo mea fidelissimus est. Ore enim ad os loquor ei; et palam, non per ænigmata et figuras, videt Deum. Rursus Moyses de se ipso testatur, quod mansuetus fuit præ cunctis habitatoribus terræ, videlicet temporis sui. Et tamen de Job Augustinus sic scribit octavodecimo de Civitate Dei: De divino sic laudatur eloquio, ut quod ad justitiam pietatemque attinet, nullus ei homo suorum temporum coæquetur. Verum ad solutionem multa possent excogitari; quæ transeo, et veritatem de incertis Deo sapientioribusque committo.
paras.en: Besides, one thing moves me: if he lived in the time of Moses, it seems strange that God bore witness of him [[1:8|that there is none like him in the earth|quod non fuit ei similis in terra]]; especially since in Numbers, speaking to Aaron and Mary of Moses, [[Num 12:6|if there be|Si fuerit]], he says, [[Num 12:6|among you a prophet of the Lord, I will appear to him in a vision, or I will speak to him in a dream|inter vos Propheta, in visione apparebo ei, vel per somnium loquar ad eum]]. [[Num 12:7|But it is not so with my servant Moses who is most faithful in all my house|At non talis servus meus Moyses, qui in omni domo mea fidelissimus est]]: [[Num 12:8|For I speak to him mouth to mouth: and plainly, and not by riddles and figures doth he see the Lord|Ore enim ad os loquor ei; et palam, non per ænigmata et figuras, videt Deum]]. Again, Moses bears witness of himself that he [[Num 12:3|was a man exceeding meek above all men that dwelt upon earth|mansuetus fuit præ cunctis habitatoribus terræ]], that is, of his own time. And yet Augustine writes thus of Job in the eighteenth book of the City of God: He is so praised by the divine word that, as regards justice and piety, no man of his own times is his equal. But many things could be devised towards a solution; these I pass over, and leave the truth of uncertain things to God and to those wiser than I.

paras.t: Nunc inquirendum quis sit auctor et scriptor libri præsentis. Quocirca dicit Gregorius: Alii Moysen, alii unum quemlibet ex Prophetis scriptorem hujus operis putant fuisse. Eos autem, qui dicunt Moysen ista descripsisse de Job tanquam de seniore et præcedente tempora Moysis, Gregorius affirmat errasse, eo quod dicat Job tempore judicum exstitisse; magisque videtur Gregorio, quod ipsemet Job hunc edidit librum: Arbitrari, inquiens, verius possumus, quod idem beatus Job, qui certamina spiritualis pugnæ sustinuit, etiam consummatæ suæ victoriæ gesta narravit. Loquitur autem de se ipso quasi de alio juxta consuetudinem Scripturarum, quemadmodum et Joannes frequenter de se quasi de alio scribit, Discipulus quem diligebat Jesus. Albertus quoque hic ait: Secundum verissimam sententiam ipse Job ista descripsit, quæ tanto certius scivit quanto ea per experimenta cognovit. Verumtamen de hac re, secundum Gregorium, non est immoderantius contendendum. Etenim ait: Quis hæc scripserit, valde supervacue quæritur, quum tamen auctor libri Spiritus Sanctus fideliter teneatur. Ipse igitur scripsit, qui scribenda dictavit ac inspiravit, videlicet Spiritus Sanctus, qui per scribentis hominis vocem, imitanda sancti Job facta nobis transmisit. Si magni cujusdam viri susceptis epistolis legeremus verba, sed quo calamo scripta essent inquireremus, ridiculum esset.
paras.en: Now we must inquire who is the author and writer of the present book. On this Gregory says: Some think that Moses, others that some one or other of the Prophets, was the writer of this work. But those who say that Moses wrote these things of Job as of one older than himself and going before Moses' times, Gregory declares to have erred, since he says that Job lived in the time of the judges; and it seems rather to Gregory that Job himself put forth this book: We may more truly suppose, he says, that the same blessed Job who bore the contests of the spiritual fight also related the deeds of his own finished victory. And he speaks of himself as of another, after the custom of the Scriptures, just as John too often writes of himself as of another: The disciple [[John 13:23|whom Jesus loved|quem diligebat Jesus]][[John 18:15||]][[John 19:26||]][[John 20:2||]]. Albert too says here: According to the truest opinion, Job himself wrote these things down, and he knew them the more surely as he learned them by experience. Yet, according to Gregory, there should be no immoderate contention about this. For he says: Who wrote these things is a very idle question, since the Holy Ghost is faithfully held to be the author of the book. He then wrote it who dictated and inspired what was to be written, that is, the Holy Ghost, who through the voice of the human writer has handed down to us the deeds of holy Job for our imitation. If we were reading the words of letters received from some great man, and yet asked with what pen they were written, it would be ridiculous.

1.title: De materia et intentione libri hujus, et an quod in libro isto narratur, fuit res gesta, vel tantum parabola.
1.title_en: On the matter and purpose of this book, and whether what is told in it really happened, or is only a parable

paras.t: In expositione sexti capituli libri hujus, refert Albertus quatuor fuisse opiniones antiquorum de isto Job. Quidam dixerunt, quod fuit homo gentilis de Esau natus, sicut præcedenti articulo patuit. Alii, quod fuit unus de sapientibus Babylonis, unusque ducum qui ab oriente venerunt, et in Babylone moratus sit post confusionem linguarum. Eos vero qui dixerunt Job de Esau descendisse, Albertus divisit in duo. Nam quidam eorum dixerunt, quod Job scripsit hunc codicem; alii, quod Moyses diu post eum. Quarta fuit opinio quorumdam, quod Job non fuit homo nec aliquid in rerum natura; sed quod in libro isto habetur, parabolice scriptum est atque inventum, ad ostendendum quod ordine justitiæ humanæ non regitur mundus per providentiam Dei, sed quod regimen providentiæ divinæ penitus dissimile sit regimini et ordini justitiæ humanæ. Hoc enim ostenditur in Job, qui simplex et rectus percussus describitur, potestatique Satanæ traditus: quod ordini justitiæ humanæ non convenit. Horum autem intellectus verborum infra clarius patefiet.
paras.en: In his exposition of the sixth chapter of this book, Albert reports that there were four opinions among the ancients about this Job. Some said that he was a gentile, born of Esau, as appeared in the preceding article. Others, that he was one of the wise men of Babylon, and one of the leaders who came from the east[[Gen 11:2||]], and that he dwelt in Babylon after the confusion of tongues. Those who said that Job descended from Esau Albert divided into two: for some of them said that Job wrote this book, others that Moses wrote it long after him. The fourth was the opinion of some who held that Job was not a man, nor anything in the nature of things; but that what is contained in this book was written and devised as a parable, to show that the world is not ruled by the providence of God according to the order of human justice, but that the rule of divine providence is wholly unlike the rule and order of human justice. For this is shown in Job, who is described as simple and upright[[1:1||]], and yet smitten[[Job 2:7||]] and given over to the power of Satan[[1:12||]][[Job 2:6||]]: which does not agree with the order of human justice. The meaning of these words will be made plainer below.

paras.t: Hinc et Thomas testatur: Fuerunt quidam, dicentes quod iste Job non fuit aliquid in rerum natura, sed quod sit quædam parabola ficta, ut esset quoddam thema ad providentiæ disputationem, sicut homines frequenter confingunt aliqua facta ad disputandum de eis. Lyra etiam refert fuisse quosdam Judæos, dicentes quod istud sit tantum parabola, et quod Moyses scripserit librum hunc; et ad declarandum conditionem virtutis patientiæ, retributionemque ejus, finxerit hominem nomine Job, et ea quæ in libro isto quasi res gestæ narrantur: quemadmodum auctor libelli qui incipit, Æthiopum terras, ad declarandum antiquitatem ac veritatem sacræ Scripturæ respectu poeticarum confictionum, finxit virginem nomine Alithiam, quod Græcum, Latine significat veritatem, et virum nomine Pseudis, id est falsus seu falsitas, ad invicem disputantes de sanctæ Scripturæ historiis poetarumque fabulis.
paras.en: Hence Thomas too testifies: There were some who said that this Job was not anything in the nature of things, but that it is a parable made up, to serve as a kind of theme for a disputation on providence, as men often make up events in order to dispute about them. Lyra also reports that there were some Jews who said that this is only a parable, and that Moses wrote this book, and that, to set forth the condition of the virtue of patience and its reward, he made up a man named Job, and the things that are told in this book as if they had happened: just as the author of the little book that begins *Æthiopum terras* [the *Ecloga Theoduli*, a medieval school-book], to set forth the antiquity and truth of Holy Scripture over against the fictions of the poets, made up a maiden named Alithia (a Greek word, which in Latin means *truth*) and a man named Pseudis, that is, false or falsehood, disputing with each other about the histories of Holy Scripture and the fables of the poets.

paras.t: Sed (ut Thomas ait) quamvis ad intentionem libri non multum referat, utrum sic vel sic dicatur, refert tamen seu differt quantum ad veritatem. Hæc namque opinio sacræ obviare videtur Scripturæ, quæ de Job sicut de homine olim veraciter exsistente eloquitur, ut quum apud Ezechielem Dominus protestatur: Terra quum peccaverit, si fuerint tres viri isti in ea, Noe, Daniel et Job, ipsi in justitia sua liberabunt animas suas; filium autem et filiam non liberabunt. Sicut ergo Noe et Daniel homines vere fuerunt, ita de Job pro certo tenendum est. Rursus, apostolus Jacobus in epistola sua, Exemplum, inquit, accipite longanimitatis, laboris et patientiæ, Prophetas, qui locuti sunt in nomine Domini. Ecce beatificamus eos qui sustinuerunt. Sufferentiam Job audistis, et finem Domini vidistis.
paras.en: But (as Thomas says) although it matters little to the purpose of the book whether it is said one way or the other, yet it matters, or makes a difference, as regards the truth. For this opinion seems to go against Holy Scripture, which speaks of Job as of a man who truly existed once, as when in Ezechiel the Lord declares: [[Ezech 14:13|when a land shall sin|Terra quum peccaverit]], [[Ezech 14:14|if these three men, Noe, Daniel, and Job, shall be in it: they shall deliver their own souls by their justice|si fuerint tres viri isti in ea, Noe, Daniel et Job, ipsi in justitia sua liberabunt animas suas]]; [[Ezech 14:16|they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters|filium autem et filiam non liberabunt]]. As therefore Noe and Daniel were truly men, so must it be held for certain of Job. Again, the apostle James in his epistle: [[Jas 5:10|Take, my brethren, for example|Exemplum]], he says, [[Jas 5:10|of suffering evil, of labour and patience, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord|accipite longanimitatis, laboris et patientiæ, Prophetas, qui locuti sunt in nomine Domini]] [Denis reads *longanimitatis*, of long-suffering]. [[Jas 5:11|Behold, we account them blessed who have endured. You have heard of the patience of Job and you have seen the end of the Lord|Ecce beatificamus eos qui sustinuerunt. Sufferentiam Job audistis, et finem Domini vidistis]].

paras.t: Porro materia libri hujus, est sufferentia et patientia sancti Job, secundum Albertum: intentio autem et finis libri seu auctoris est, ostendere qualiter actus humani providentiæ divinæ subjaceant, et quomodo res humanæ gubernentur a Deo. Dicit autem circa hoc Thomas: Tota intentio libri istius circa hoc versatur, ut per rationes probabiles ostendatur res humanas a divina providentia regi. Sed istud dictum B. Thomæ cuidam non placet, eo quod totus hic liber procedat per modum disputationis inter Job et ejus amicos: intentio autem contra alium disputantis, non est probare aut declarare id in quo cum eo concordat; sed illo pro vero supposito, id in quo ab eo dissentit. Quum ergo omnes isti contra Job disputantes, concesserint actus hominum divina providentia regi, intentio Job non est id declarare, sed aliquid in quo ab eis dissensit, videlicet, quod non sic reguntur a Deo ut illi putabant.
paras.en: Now the matter of this book, according to Albert, is the sufferance and patience of holy Job; and the purpose and end of the book, or of its author, is to show how human acts are subject to divine providence, and how human affairs are governed by God. On this Thomas says: The whole purpose of this book turns on this, that it be shown by probable reasons that human affairs are ruled by divine providence. But this saying of blessed Thomas does not please a certain writer, because this whole book proceeds by way of a disputation between Job and his friends; and the purpose of one who disputes against another is not to prove or set forth that in which he agrees with him, but, taking that as true, that in which he dissents from him. Since, then, all those who dispute against Job granted that the acts of men are ruled by divine providence, Job's purpose is not to set this forth, but something in which he dissented from them, namely, that they are not ruled by God in the way they supposed.

paras.t: Verum objectio ista procedit contra verba, non contra mentem Thomæ, qui in principio expositionis primi capituli dicit: Intentio tota libri hujus ordinatur ad ostendendum qualiter res humanæ providentia divina regantur. Ex quo clarissime constat, quod Thomas non voluit simpliciter dicere intentionem auctoris seu libri hujus esse, ostendere quod humana regantur a Deo, sed qualiter gubernentur ab eo. Unde et forma verborum Thomæ, quam alter impugnat, faciliter veraciterque salvatur: quoniam absolute loquendo, idem est ipsa res et veritas ejus, loquendo de veritate naturæ: sic enim ens et verum convertuntur, nec verum enti reale quid superaddit. Quum igitur Thomas dicit, Intentio libri est, ostendere quod res humanæ divina providentia gubernantur, tantum est dicere ac si dicat: Intentio libri est, ostendere quod res humanæ providentia divina reguntur, secundum quod veritas ipsa se habet, non eo modo quo aliqui errando putabant.
paras.en: But this objection goes against the words, not against the mind of Thomas, who at the beginning of his exposition of the first chapter says: The whole purpose of this book is directed to showing how human affairs are ruled by divine providence. From this it is most clearly established that Thomas did not mean to say simply that the purpose of the author, or of this book, is to show that human things are ruled by God, but how they are governed by him. Hence even the form of Thomas's words, which the other attacks, is easily and truly upheld: for, speaking absolutely, a thing and its truth are the same, speaking of the truth of nature [that is, the truth a thing has in its own being]: for thus being and the true are convertible, and the true adds nothing real to being. When, then, Thomas says, The purpose of the book is to show that human affairs are governed by divine providence, it is as much as to say: The purpose of the book is to show that human affairs are ruled by divine providence as the truth itself stands, not in the way that some supposed in their error.

paras.t: Præterea, præfatus in argumento suo aliquid ponit, quod inquisitionem requirit majorem. Siquidem ait, quod licet amici Job dicerent actus hominum providentia regi divina, tamen tenebant, quod adversa mundi non accidunt homini nisi propter ejus demerita seu mala præterita, nec prospera nisi propter præcedentia opera bona: quod constat esse erroneum. An dictum istud sit verum, videlicet, an amici Job ita senserunt, non est tam certum ut aliqui arbitrantur. Albertus quoque vir subtilissimus, ex verbis amicorum Job ostendit oppositum, prout infra clarebit. Ideo pro nunc inde pertranseo.
paras.en: Besides, the writer just mentioned lays down in his argument something that calls for closer inquiry. For he says that, although Job's friends said that the acts of men are ruled by divine providence, yet they held that the adversities of the world befall a man only on account of his demerits, or past evils, and prosperity only on account of good works gone before: which is plainly erroneous. Whether this saying is true, that is, whether Job's friends thought so, is not as certain as some suppose. Albert too, a most subtle man, shows the opposite from the words of Job's friends, as will appear below. So for now I pass on from it.

paras.t: Advertendum autem pro intellectu dictorum, quod sicut beatissimus Augustinus in libris de Civitate Dei, sapientissime docet, ab exordio generis humani cœperunt civitas Dei civitasque diaboli, id est congregatio hominum bonorum et electorum, et collectio impiorum et reproborum. Cain namque primogenitus protoplastorum parentum reprobus et injustus, occidit innocentem Abel: quo facto, recessit a suis parentibus, moratusque est in parte terræ distante ab eis, juxta illud Genesis, Egressus Cain a facie Domini, habitavit profugus in terra ad orientalem partem Eden. Deinde Adam genuit Seth electum a Deo, in cujus posteritate cultus Dei diu remansit, cujus et posteri a primo parente in divinis edocti sunt. Cain vero et posteri ejus vitiis intenderunt. Non tamen leguntur homines ad idololatriam ante diluvium declinasse: ex quo consequens est, quod unum solum verum summumque Deum esse noverunt. Paulatim tamen sic obtenebrati ac victi sunt vitiis, quod omnis caro humana viam suam corrupit; nec Dei providentiam judiciumque pensaverunt, quamvis forte ea non negaverunt: sicut et modo multi sunt Christiani tam excæcati et vitiose viventes, quasi nec providentia Dei, nec futurum esset judicium, quamvis fide informi credant hujusmodi.
paras.en: For the understanding of what has been said, it should be observed that, as most blessed Augustine most wisely teaches in the books of the City of God, from the beginning of the human race there began the city of God and the city of the devil, that is, the gathering of good and elect men, and the assembly of the wicked and reprobate. For Cain, the firstborn of our first parents[[Gen 4:1||]], reprobate and unjust, slew innocent Abel[[Gen 4:8||]]; and after this he withdrew from his parents and dwelt in a part of the earth far from them, according to that text of Genesis: [[Gen 4:16|Cain went out from the face of the Lord, and dwelt as a fugitive on the earth at the east side of Eden|Egressus Cain a facie Domini, habitavit profugus in terra ad orientalem partem Eden]]. Then Adam begot Seth, chosen by God[[Gen 4:25||]][[Gen 5:3||]], in whose posterity the worship of God long remained, and whose descendants were taught divine things by the first parent. But Cain and his descendants gave themselves to vices. Yet we do not read that men turned aside to idolatry before the flood: from which it follows that they knew that there is one only, true and supreme God. Little by little, however, they were so darkened and overcome by vices that [[Gen 6:12|all flesh had corrupted its way|omnis caro humana viam suam corrupit]]; nor did they weigh God's providence and judgment, though perhaps they did not deny them: just as now there are many Christians so blinded and living so viciously, as though there were neither providence of God nor judgment to come, although with unformed faith [that is, faith without charity] they believe such things.

paras.t: Post diluvium vero ad idololatriam sunt prolapsi, et tandem in tantum excæcati sunt multi, ut vel unum verum summum Deum esse non scirent nec crederent; vel si hoc scirent aut crederent, tamen divinam providentiam denegarent. Nec vulgus dumtaxat et indocti, sed et qui inquisitioni veritatis operam dederunt, puta philosophi quidam, tales fuerunt, omnia casualiter fieri opinantes, sicut de Epicureis et antiquis Aristoteles narrat. Posteriores vero philosophi, profundius ordinem rerum, cursum stellarum, mundi dispositionem ac statum scrutantes, invenerunt unum esse primum universorum principium: quorum quidam dixerunt sola superiora atque cœlestia ejus providentiæ subjacere, ac regi ab eo; alii vero, omnia naturalia. Sed de rebus actibusque humanis multiplex fuit inter eos error atque opinio, utrum et quomodo esset de eis providentia, dispositio ac judicium Dei, præsertim quia difficile fuit eis videre quomodo infallibilitas præscientiæ Dei et libertas arbitrii simul starent. Et quia videbant, quod in vita præsenti boni opprimuntur a malis, et impii prosperantur, virtuosi adversitatibus affliguntur, ita quod in humanis eventibus nullus certus ordo apparet (non enim bonis semper eveniunt bona, nec malis semper mala; nec iterum bonis semper mala, nec malis semper accidunt bona, sed indifferenter bonis et malis bona et mala); hinc mota sunt corda multorum, quod actus humani non disponuntur per providentiam Dei. Quorum error devenit ad hoc, quod vel fortunæ vel casui, vel fato eos attribuerunt: qui error nocentissimus fuit hominibus. Inde enim venit irrefrenata peccandi libertas; omnisque timor, amor et reverentia Dei discessit. Ideo præcipua sanctorum Patrum diligentia fuit istum exstirpare errorem, et demonstrare omnia divinitus gubernari, ita quod nullum malum permanet impunitum, nec aliquod bonum irremuneratum. Sed et aliqui præclariores philosophi hoc aliqualiter per sapientiam acquisitam docuisse leguntur. Hinc et sanctus Job in libro suo id potissime docere intendit et docet, ac probat juxta modum prætactum.
paras.en: After the flood, however, they fell away into idolatry, and at length many were so far blinded that either they did not know or believe that there is one true and supreme God, or, if they knew or believed this, they yet denied divine providence. And not only the common people and the unlearned, but also those who gave themselves to the search for truth, such as certain philosophers, were of this kind, holding that all things happen by chance, as Aristotle relates of the Epicureans and the ancients. But later philosophers, searching more deeply into the order of things, the course of the stars, and the arrangement and state of the world, found that there is one first principle of all things: and some of them said that only the higher and heavenly things are subject to his providence and ruled by him; others, all natural things. But concerning human affairs and acts there was manifold error and opinion among them, whether and how there was providence, disposition and judgment of God over them, especially because it was hard for them to see how the infallibility of God's foreknowledge and the freedom of the will could stand together. And because they saw that in the present life the good are oppressed by the wicked, and the ungodly prosper, and the virtuous are afflicted with adversities, so that no sure order appears in human events (for good things do not always befall the good, nor evil things always the wicked; nor again do evil things always befall the good, nor good things always the wicked, but good and evil befall good and wicked alike); hence the hearts of many were moved to think that human acts are not ordered by the providence of God. Their error came to this, that they ascribed them to fortune, or to chance, or to fate: an error most harmful to men. For from it comes unbridled freedom to sin, and all fear, love and reverence of God departs. Therefore the chief care of the holy Fathers was to root out this error, and to show that all things are governed by God, so that no evil remains unpunished, nor any good unrewarded. And some of the more eminent philosophers too are read to have taught this in some measure by acquired wisdom [that is, by natural reason, as distinct from revelation]. Hence holy Job too in his book means above all to teach this, and does teach it, and proves it in the way touched on above [the margin beside these last words prints what seems to read *Job xxiii*, with no verse; it fits no quotation here].

1.title: De quibusdam præambulis documentis, ex verbis sancti Gregorii.
1.title_en: On certain preliminary teachings, from the words of St. Gregory

paras.t: Præmittit B. Gregorius expositioni voluminis hujus quædam utilia documenta, ad totius libri intelligentiam opportuna: Quædam, inquiens, historica expositione transcurrimus, id est, litteraliter breviter explanamus; et per allegoriam quædam typica investigatione scrutamur, illa videlicet quæ figuraliter de Christo per allegoriam exponuntur, in quibus Job fuit Christi figura; quædam per solam moralitatem discutimus; nonnulla autem per cuncta hæc sollicite exquirentes tripliciter indagamus, id est, litteraliter, allegorice moraliterque exponimus. Nam primo fundamenta historiæ ponimus; deinde per significationem typicam, figuralem seu allegoricam, in arcem fidei fabricam mentis erigimus, id est, animæ contemplationem ad fidei mysteria contuenda levamus: allegoria enim instruit quid credendum. Postremo per moralitatem spirituale expositionum istarum ædificium quasi superducto pulchro colore vestimus. Quos sensus ori lectoris interno tanquam fercula exhibemus, ut ejus fastidia repellamus, qui dum sibi multa oblata considerat, quod elegantius discernit, assumat. Quid etenim sunt veritatis eloquia, nisi reficiendæ mentis edulia?
paras.en: Blessed Gregory sets before his exposition of this book certain useful teachings, fit for the understanding of the whole book. Some things, he says, we run through by historical exposition, that is, we explain them briefly according to the letter; some we search out by allegory, with a typical investigation, namely those that are expounded figuratively of Christ by allegory, in which Job was a figure of Christ; some we discuss by the moral sense alone; and some, searching them out carefully by all these ways, we investigate threefold, that is, we expound them literally, allegorically and morally. For first we lay the foundations of the history; then by the typical, figurative or allegorical signification we raise the building of the mind into a citadel of faith, that is, we lift up the soul's contemplation to behold the mysteries of faith: for allegory teaches what is to be believed. Lastly, by the moral sense we clothe the spiritual building of these expositions as with a fair colour laid over it. These senses we set before the inward mouth of the reader like dishes, so as to drive away his distaste, so that, when he considers the many things offered him, he may take what he judges the finer. For what are the words of truth but food to refresh the mind?

paras.t: Aliqua vero litteraliter intelligi nequeunt, quoniam sic accepta, non ædificationem, sed errorem legentibus gignerent, ut quum dicitur, Sub quo (scilicet Deo) curvantur qui portant orbem: et de tanto viro, puta beato Job, quis nesciat quod nequaquam vanas poetarum fabulas sequitur, ut mundi molem portari giganteis putetur sudore? Et rursus persecutionibus pressus, ait: Elegit suspendium anima mea, et mortem ossa mea, quasi vir tantæ virtutis voluerit propter adversa suspendio vitam finire.
paras.en: Some things, however, cannot be understood according to the letter, since, taken so, they would beget in readers not edification but error: as when it is said, [[Job 9:13|under whom|Sub quo]] (that is, God) [[Job 9:13|they stoop that bear up the world|curvantur qui portant orbem]]: and of so great a man, blessed Job, who does not know that he by no means follows the vain fables of the poets, so as to suppose that the mass of the world is borne up by the sweat of giants [the poets' tale of Atlas]? And again, pressed by persecutions, he says: [[Job 7:15|my soul rather chooseth hanging, and my bones death|Elegit suspendium anima mea, et mortem ossa mea]], as though a man of such virtue had wished to end his life by hanging because of his adversities.

paras.t: Aliquando ipsa verba litteræ se impugnant, ne ad litteram intelligantur. Ait namque: Pereat dies in qua natus sum; et, Occupet eum caligo. Qui dies jam evolutus, stare non poterat: quomodo ergo hunc caligine involvi optabat? Qui iterum dicit, Peccavi, quid faciam tibi, o custos hominum? Et: Consumere me vis peccatis adolescentiæ meæ. Et tamen alia responsione subjungit: Neque enim reprehendit me cor meum in omni vita mea. Quæ verba dum sic invicem collata convenire stareque nequeunt, aliud quid in se, quod quæratur, ostendunt.
paras.en: Sometimes the very words of the letter fight against themselves, so that they may not be understood according to the letter. For he says: [[Job 3:3|Let the day perish wherein I was born|Pereat dies in qua natus sum]]; and: [[Job 3:5|let a mist overspread it|Occupet eum caligo]]. That day, already rolled away, could not stand still: how then did he wish it to be wrapped in mist? He says again: [[Job 7:20|I have sinned: what shall I do to thee, O keeper of men?|Peccavi, quid faciam tibi, o custos hominum?]] And: Thou [[Job 13:26|wilt consume me for the sins of my youth|Consumere me vis peccatis adolescentiæ meæ]]. And yet in another answer he adds: [[Job 27:6|for my heart doth not reprehend me in all my life|Neque enim reprehendit me cor meum in omni vita mea]]. Since these words, set side by side, cannot agree and stand together, they show that there is something else in them to be sought.

paras.t: Aliquando qui sensum litteralem omittit, propositum sibi lumen veritatis abscondit: ut quum de operibus misericordiæ suæ testatur: Si comedi buccellam meam solus, etc. Divinus etenim sermo sicut mysteriis prudentes exercet, sic plerumque superficie simplices refovet. Habet in publico unde parvulos nutriat; servat in secreto unde mentes sublimium in admiratione suspendat. Est quippe sacra Scriptura ut fluvius planus et altus sive profundus, in quo et agnus ambulet, et elephas natet.
paras.en: Sometimes he who leaves aside the literal sense hides from himself the light of truth set before him: as when Job bears witness of his works of mercy: [[Job 31:17|If I have eaten my morsel alone|Si comedi buccellam meam solus]], etc. For the divine word, as it exercises the wise with mysteries, so for the most part it refreshes the simple with its surface. It has in the open wherewith to nourish little ones; it keeps in secret wherewith to hold the minds of the lofty rapt in wonder. For Holy Scripture is like a river both shallow and deep, in which the lamb may walk and the elephant swim.

paras.t: Insuper Gregorius de se ait: Fortasse divinæ providentiæ consilium fuit, ut percussum Job percussus, videlicet crebris viscerum doloribus cruciatus, horis momentisque omnibus fracta stomachi virtute lassatus, lentis quoque et continuis febribus anhelans, exponerem, et flagellati mentem melius per flagella sentirem.
paras.en: Moreover Gregory says of himself: Perhaps it was the counsel of divine providence that I, smitten, should expound the smitten Job (that is, tormented with frequent pains in the bowels, worn out at every hour and moment by the broken strength of my stomach, gasping too with slow and continual fevers), and that I should better perceive through scourges the mind of one who was scourged.

paras.t: Præterea dicit Gregorius: Omnis homo eo ipso quo homo est, intelligere suum debet auctorem. Conditi autem, Deum considerare negleximus. Adhibita sunt præcepta; præceptis obtemperare noluimus. Adjunguntur exempla; ipsa quoque exempla imitari declinavimus, quæ edidisse nobis patres sub lege positos cernimus. Unde ad confutandam impudentiam nostram, gentilis homo ad exemplum deducitur: ut, quia obedire homo legi sub lege positus despicit, ejus saltem comparatione evigilet, qui sine lege (scilicet scripta) legaliter vixit. Erranti igitur homini data est lex; erranti vero sub lege adducitur testimonium eorum qui extra legem sunt: ut, quia conditionis nostræ ordinem servare noluimus, præceptis admoneremur; quia præceptis obedire contempsimus, exemplis confunderemur. Itaque ex vita gentilium redarguitur vita sub lege etiam evangelica positorum, atque ex actione sæcularium confunditur vita religiosorum promissa non observantium.
paras.en: Further, Gregory says: Every man, by the very fact that he is a man, ought to understand his Maker. But, once made, we neglected to consider God. Precepts were applied; we would not obey the precepts. Examples are added; those examples too we declined to imitate, which we see that the fathers set under the Law gave us. Hence, to confound our shamelessness, a gentile is brought forward as an example: so that, since man set under the Law scorns to obey the Law, he may at least wake up by comparison with one who lived lawfully without the Law (that is, the written Law). To man in his error, then, the Law was given; and to man erring under the Law is brought the witness of those who are outside the Law: so that, since we would not keep the order of our condition, we might be admonished by precepts; and since we scorned to obey the precepts, we might be put to shame by examples. And so by the life of the gentiles the life of those set under the Law, even the Law of the Gospel, is rebuked, and by the conduct of people in the world the life of religious who do not keep what they have vowed is put to shame.

paras.t: Porro Redemptor noster sicut ad redemptionem Judæorum et gentilium venit, ita se prophetari Judæorum et gentilium vocibus voluit, ut per utrumque populum prædiceretur, qui pro utroque populo aliquando pateretur. Sanctus autem Job summis virtutibus fultus, sibi notus erat et Deo: qui si non flagellaretur, a nobis nullatenus perfecte cognosceretur. Virtus quippe ejus etiam in quiete se exercitavit, sed virtutis opinio flagellis commota fragravit. Sicut enim unguenta late non redolent, nisi commota; et sicut aromata fragrantiam suam non nisi incendantur, expandunt: ita sancti viri omne quod virtutibus redolent, in tribulationibus innotescunt. Hinc dicitur in Psalmo: In die mandavit Dominus misericordiam suam, et nocte declaravit eam. Misericordia enim Domini in die mandatur, quoniam in tranquillo tempore cognoscendo percipitur. In nocte vero declaratur, quia donum quod in tranquillitate sumitur, tribulationibus manifestatur.
paras.en: Again, as our Redeemer came for the redemption of Jews and gentiles, so he willed to be foretold by the voices of Jews and gentiles, so that he who was one day to suffer for both peoples might be foretold by both peoples. Now holy Job, upheld by the highest virtues, was known to himself and to God: and had he not been scourged, he would by no means have been perfectly known by us. For his virtue exercised itself even in quiet, but the fame of his virtue, stirred by scourges, gave forth its fragrance. For as ointments do not give out their smell far unless they are stirred, and as spices do not spread their fragrance unless they are burned, so holy men make known in tribulations all the sweetness of their virtues. Hence it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 41:9|In the daytime the Lord hath commanded his mercy|In die mandavit Dominus misericordiam suam]], and in the night he hath declared it [Denis, with Gregory, reads *et nocte declaravit eam*, where the Vulgate has *et nocte canticum ejus*, and a canticle to him in the night]. For the mercy of the Lord is commanded in the day, because in a time of calm it is received in knowing it; but it is declared in the night, because the gift received in calm is made manifest in tribulations.

paras.t: Sed subtilius perscrutandum, cur vir tantæ perfectionis tot flagella sustinuit. Et respondendum, quod quum omnia virtutum mandata perficeret, unum ei deerat, ut scilicet flagellatus etiam gratias agere sciret. Notum erat quia servire Deo inter dona et prospera noverat; sed dignum fuit, ut districtio severitatis inquireret an et inter flagella Deo devotus maneret. Pœna namque interrogat ac demonstrat, si quietus quis Deum veraciter amat. Fieri autem Dominus benigne permisit, quod inique diabolus postulavit.
paras.en: But we must search out more closely why a man of such perfection bore so many scourges. And the answer is that, while he fulfilled all the commandments of the virtues, one thing was lacking to him: that he should know how to give thanks even when scourged. It was known that he knew how to serve God amid gifts and prosperity; but it was fitting that the strictness of severity should inquire whether he would stay devoted to God amid scourges too. For pain questions a man, and shows whether, when at peace, he truly loves God. And the Lord in kindness allowed to be done what the devil in wickedness asked for.

paras.t: Sed libet inter hæc mira divinæ dispensationis opera cernere, quomodo a principio generis humani Deus viros virtutibus variis decoratos, quasi stellas varia luce fulgentes, ad illuminandam noctem vitæ præsentis, id est vitam hanc vitiis tenebrosam, transmisit, et mittit quousque in fine Dominus tanquam verus Lucifer oriatur sive appareat. Ad ostendendam namque innocentiam venit Abel; ad docendam actionis munditiam venit Enoch; ad insinuandam longanimitatem spei et operis venit Noe; ad manifestandam obedientiam venit Abraham; ad demonstrandam conjugalis vitæ castimoniam venit Isaac; ad insinuandam laboris tolerantiam venit Jacob; ad retribuendum bonum pro malo venit Joseph; ad ostendendam mansuetudinem venit Moyses; ad informandam contra adversa fiduciam venit Josue; ad ostendendam inter flagella patientiam venit Job. Sancti isti ceterique electi, qui Salvatorem præcesserunt, rebus et vocibus hunc prophetando promiserunt. Nullus etenim justus hujusmodi fuit qui non ejus per figuram nuntius exstitit. Hinc beatus Job, qui tanta Christi incarnationis mysteria protulit, eum quem voce dixit, conversatione signavit; et per ea quæ pertulit, quæ ille passurus esset, ostendit. Tantoque verius passionis Christi sacramenta prædixit, quanto hæc non loquendo tantum, sed patiendo etiam prophetavit.
paras.en: But it is good, amid these things, to behold the wonderful works of the divine dispensation: how from the beginning of the human race God has sent men adorned with various virtues, like stars shining with various light, to light up the night of the present life, that is, this life darkened by vices; and he sends them until at the end the Lord rises, or appears, as the true Lucifer [that is, the morning star]. For to show innocence came Abel[[Matt 23:35||]][[Heb 11:4||]]; to teach purity of action came Enoch[[Gen 5:22||]][[Gen 5:24||]]; to suggest long-suffering of hope and of work came Noe[[Gen 6:9||]][[Gen 6:22||]]; to make obedience manifest came Abraham[[Heb 11:8||]][[Heb 11:17||]]; to show the chastity of married life came Isaac[[Gen 24:67||]][[Gen 49:31||]]; to suggest the bearing of labour came Jacob[[Gen 31:40||]] [the margin's reference here is badly printed, with the verse 9; Gen 31:40 tells of Jacob's labour]; to repay good for evil came Joseph[[Gen 45:5||]]; to show meekness came Moses[[Num 12:3||]]; to form confidence against adversity came Josue[[Ecclus 46:1||]]; to show patience amid scourges came Job[[1:12||]]. These saints, and the other elect who went before the Saviour, promised him by prophesying with deeds and words. For there was no just man of this kind who was not his herald in figure. Hence blessed Job, who uttered such great mysteries of Christ's incarnation, signified by his manner of life him of whom he spoke with his voice; and by what he bore he showed what Christ was to suffer. And he foretold the mysteries of Christ's passion the more truly, in that he prophesied them not only by speaking but also by suffering.

1.title: Expositio litteralis primi capituli libri Job: Vir erat in terra Hus, nomine Job.
1.title_en: Literal exposition of the first chapter of the book of Job: There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job

paras.t: Vir erat in terra Hus, nomine Job. Primo historia quædam inducitur, quæ totius sequentis disputationis velut fundamentum et thema est, ad declarandum qualiter actus hominum providentia gubernentur divina. Porro de persona, nomine, cognatione et terra Job, dicta sunt plurima primo articulo: unde ex dictis ibidem patet intelligentia hujus particulæ textus. Fuit autem Job vir triplici virilitatis perfectione, videlicet perfectione animi per virtutum constantiam, perfectione naturæ per virentem germinationem, perfectione sexus. Sexus namque masculinus perfectior est, et ad sustinendas molestias fortior: ideo decuit personam, in qua patientiæ exemplum præclarum fuerat demonstrandum, esse sexus virilis. Denique secundum Gregorium, perfectione animi vir vocatur, qui contra biformes fortunæ insultus uniformi mentis constantia militat: qui scilicet nec prosperis vane extollitur, nec adversis mente dejicitur, sed regia via semper incedit. Hinc ad Eugenium Papam ait Bernardus: Magnus est cui dignitas sæculi si arrisit, non irrisit; nec minor est illo, qui incidens in adversa, non excidit a sapientia. Quam perfectionem adepta est sancta Anna, de qua primo Regum habetur, Vultus ejus non sunt amplius in diversa mutati; et beatissimus pater noster S. Martinus, de quo testatur Severus, quod nemo illum unquam vidit tristem aut dissolutum. Itaque et nos conemur taliter viri esse: quod erit, si passiones fuerint reformatæ, omnesque animarum nostrarum affectiones in Deum stabiliter ordinatæ.
paras.en: [[1:1|There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job|Vir erat in terra Hus, nomine Job]]. First a certain history is set down, which is as it were the foundation and theme of the whole disputation that follows, to make plain how the acts of men are governed by divine providence. Of the person, name, kindred and land of Job a great deal was said in the first article, so the meaning of this little part of the text is clear from what was said there. Now Job was a man with a threefold perfection of manhood: perfection of soul through constancy in the virtues, perfection of nature through flourishing fruitfulness, and perfection of sex [Denis plays on *vir*, “man”, *virilitas*, “manhood”, *virtus*, “virtue”, and *virens*, “flourishing”]. For the male sex is the more perfect, and the stronger for bearing hardships; and so it was fitting that the person in whom a shining example of patience was to be shown should be of the male sex. Further, according to Gregory, he is called a man (*vir*) for perfection of soul who fights against the twofold assaults of fortune with an unchanging constancy of mind: that is, who is neither vainly lifted up by prosperity nor cast down in mind by adversity, but always walks the royal road. Hence Bernard says to Pope Eugene: Great is he on whom the dignity of the world has smiled without mocking him [*arrisit, non irrisit*, a play on “smiled on” and “laughed at”]; nor is he less who, falling into adversity, has not fallen away from wisdom. This perfection holy Anna attained, of whom it is said in the First Book of Kings: [[1 Kings 1:18|her countenance was no more changed|Vultus ejus non sunt amplius in diversa mutati]]; and our most blessed father St Martin, of whom Severus testifies that no one ever saw him sad or unbridled. Let us too, then, strive to be men in this way: and so we shall be, if our passions have been reformed and all the affections of our souls steadily ordered towards God.

paras.t: Præterea secundum Gregorium, terra in qua Job habitavit, exprimitur, ut ex hoc perfectio suæ virtutis amplius commendetur. Hus namque est terra gentilium: sicque dum scribitur inter malos fuisse moratus, perfectior declaratur. Item Gregorius: Neque enim valde laudabile est, bonum esse cum bonis, sed bonum esse cum malis. Quemadmodum autem gravioris est culpæ, inter bonos bonum non esse; ita immensi præconii est, etiam inter malos bonum consistere.
paras.en: Moreover, according to Gregory, the land in which Job dwelt is named so that the perfection of his virtue may be the more commended by it. For Hus is a land of the Gentiles; and so, when it is written that he lived among the wicked, he is shown to be the more perfect. Gregory again: For it is not very praiseworthy to be good with the good, but to be good with the wicked. For as it is the graver fault not to be good among the good, so it is a matter of immense praise to stand good even among the wicked.

paras.t: Et erat vir ille simplex, triplici simplicitate, secundum Albertum (per quem in toto hoc opere intelligo Albertum Magnum ordinis Prædicatorum), videlicet simplicitate intentionis: quoniam in omnibus quæ agebat, unum summum bonum intendebat. De qua simplicitate loquitur Christus, Si oculus tuus fuerit simplex, totum corpus tuum lucidum erit: cui simplicitati opponitur duplicitas cordis volentium Deo et mundo placere, nuncque gaudere cum sæculo, et postea regnare cum Christo; cum tamen ipse testatus sit: Nemo potest duobus dominis servire. Unde Ecclesiasticus quoque asserit: Væ peccatori ingredienti terram duabus viis. Et iterum: Ne accesseris ad Deum duplici corde. Quantum hæc bona simplicitas placeat Deo, patet ex eo quod Salomon profitetur: Cum simplicibus sermocinatio ejus. Ad Philippenses quoque ait Apostolus: Sitis sine querela, simplices filii Dei. Secundo, fuit simplex simplicitate virtutis in generali: quæ simplicitas consistit in hoc, quod virtus est ex una sola totaque causa, secundum divinum Dionysium atque Philosophum, vitium vero ex causa multiplici. Huic simplicitati opponitur multiplicitas peccati, juxta illud secundi Paralipomenon: Peccavi super numerum arenæ maris; multiplicatæ sunt iniquitates meæ. Tertio, simplicitate prudentiæ, quæ est sine plica astutiæ, dolositatis et tergiversationis ad malum. Itaque accipitur hic simplicitas non ut opponitur intellectus perspicacitati, sed dolositati. Est namque et mala ac asinina simplicitas per debitæ considerationis defectum, ad quam pertinere potest illud Proverbiorum: Simplex credit omni verbo; astutus considerat gressus suos. Potestque ibi astutia sumi in bono.
paras.en: [[1:1|and that man was simple|Et erat vir ille simplex]], with a threefold simplicity, according to Albert (by whom throughout this work I mean Albert the Great, of the Order of Preachers). First, by simplicity of intention, since in all that he did he intended the one supreme good. Of this simplicity Christ speaks: [[Matt 6:22|If thy eye be single, thy whole body shall be lightsome|Si oculus tuus fuerit simplex, totum corpus tuum lucidum erit]]. To this simplicity is opposed the doubleness of heart of those who wish to please God and the world, to rejoice with the world now and afterwards to reign with Christ; though he himself has testified: [[Matt 6:24|No man can serve two masters|Nemo potest duobus dominis servire]]. Hence Ecclesiasticus too declares: [[Ecclus 2:14|Woe|Væ]] [[Ecclus 2:14|to the sinner that goeth on the earth two ways|peccatori ingredienti terram duabus viis]]. And again: [[Ecclus 1:36|come not to him with a double heart|Ne accesseris ad Deum duplici corde]]. How much this good simplicity pleases God is clear from what Solomon professes: [[Prov 3:32|his communication is with the simple|Cum simplicibus sermocinatio ejus]]. The Apostle too says to the Philippians: [[Phil 2:15|That you may be blameless and sincere children of God|Sitis sine querela, simplices filii Dei]]. Secondly, he was simple with the simplicity of virtue in general: this simplicity consists in this, that virtue comes from one single and entire cause, according to the divine Dionysius and the Philosopher, but vice from a manifold cause [that is, an act is good only when everything in it is right, but evil from any one defect]. To this simplicity is opposed the multiplicity of sin, according to that word of the Second Book of Paralipomenon: I have sinned above the number of the sand of the sea; my iniquities are multiplied [these words are from the Prayer of Manasses, printed in the Vulgate after the Second Book of Paralipomenon; it is not in the Douay-Rheims text used in this app]. Thirdly, with the simplicity of prudence, which is without the fold of craft, deceit and shuffling towards evil [Denis takes *simplex*, “simple”, as *sine plica*, “without a fold”]. So simplicity is taken here not as it is opposed to keenness of understanding, but as it is opposed to deceitfulness. For there is also a bad and asinine simplicity, through lack of due consideration, to which that word of Proverbs may belong: [[Prov 14:15|The innocent believeth every word: the discreet man considereth his steps|Simplex credit omni verbo; astutus considerat gressus suos]] [Denis reads *simplex*, “the simple man”, where the Vulgate has *innocens*]. And there craftiness [*astutus*, “crafty”, which the Douay-Rheims renders “discreet”] may be taken in a good sense.

paras.t: Fuit autem et rectus, id est justus affectu et opere. Rectitudo equidem proprie ad justitiam pertinet, quæ in æqualitate consistit, juxta illud Isaiæ: Semita justi recta est. Quocontra de impiis Salomon ait: Relinquunt iter rectum, et ambulant per vias tenebrosas. Porro recta itinera sunt divina præcepta, sine vitiorum obliquitate ad beatitudinem veram ducentia: per quæ justi pede ambulant inoffenso, pravi vero in eis labuntur, juxta illud Osee: Rectæ viæ Domini, et justi ambulabunt in eis; prævaricatores autem corruent in eis. Denique Ambrosius ait: Rectus est qui suam voluntatem conformat divinæ, volens de omni re quod Deus vult eum velle, et ex eadem caritate qua Deus, vult quod vult. Anselmus quoque: Justitia, inquit, est rectitudo sola mente perceptibilis. Ex quo certum est, quod rectitudo ad justitiam spectet. Itaque rectus est qui per lineas æquitatis in actibus suis procedit. Rectum namque est, ut etiam a Platone asseritur, cujus medium non exit ab extremis. Extrema vero operationis humanæ sunt: prima principia in operabilibus, sicut est illud Salvatoris in Evangelio, Quæcumque vultis ut faciant vobis homines, facite eis; et illud Tobiæ, Quod ab alio oderis fieri tibi, vide ne aliquando alii facias; et ultimus finis, puta æterna felicitas. Job ergo et omnis justus dicitur rectus, quoniam in actibus suis processit a principiis operabilium, absque declinatione ad culpam, ad ultimum finem.
paras.en: He was also [[1:1|upright|rectus]], that is, just in affection and in deed. Uprightness [*rectitudo*, “rightness” or “straightness”] belongs properly to justice, which consists in equality, according to that word of Isaias: [[Is 26:7|The way of the just is right|Semita justi recta est]]. Whereas of the wicked Solomon says: [[Prov 2:13|leave the right way, and walk by dark ways|Relinquunt iter rectum, et ambulant per vias tenebrosas]]. Now the right roads are the divine precepts, which lead to true beatitude without the crookedness of vices: by them the just walk with unstumbling foot, while the wicked slip in them, according to that word of Osee: [[Osee 14:10|the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them: but the transgressors shall fall in them|Rectæ viæ Domini, et justi ambulabunt in eis; prævaricatores autem corruent in eis]]. Ambrose, further, says: He is upright who conforms his own will to the divine, willing in every matter what God wills him to will, and willing what he wills out of the same charity as God. Anselm too: Justice, he says, is rightness perceptible to the mind alone. From this it is certain that uprightness concerns justice. And so he is upright who goes forward in his acts along the lines of equity. For the straight [*rectum*, the same word as “upright”], as Plato too asserts, is that whose middle does not stray from its extremes [that is, from the line between its two ends]. Now the extremes of human action are, first, the first principles in matters of action, such as that word of the Saviour in the Gospel: [[Matt 7:12|whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do you also to them|Quæcumque vultis ut faciant vobis homines, facite eis]]; and that of Tobias: [[Tob 4:16|See thou never do to another what thou wouldst hate to have done to thee by another|Quod ab alio oderis fieri tibi, vide ne aliquando alii facias]]; and, second, the last end, namely eternal happiness. Job therefore, and every just man, is called upright, since in his acts he went forward from the principles of action to the last end without turning aside to sin.

paras.t: At vero secundum Gregorium, quidam ita sunt simplices, ut quid sit rectum, ignorent; sed eo veræ simplicitatis innocentiam deserunt, quo ad virtutem rectitudinis non assurgunt. Propter quod Paulus ait: Volo vos sapientes esse in bono, simplices autem in malo. Et ipsemet Christus: Estote prudentes sicut serpentes, et simplices sicut columbæ; ut scilicet simplicitatem columbæ astutia serpentis instrueret, et serpentis astutiam columbæ simplicitas temperaret. Hinc Spiritus Sanctus non in specie columbæ tantum, sed et in igne apparuit. Per columbam namque simplicitas, per ignem zelus exprimitur. Qui autem repleti sunt Spiritu Sancto, sic mansuetudini simplicitatis deserviunt, ut contra delinquentium culpas etiam zelo rectitudinis accendantur. Hinc et Salomon duo ista conjungit, dicens: Qui recti sunt, habitabunt in terra, et simplices permanebunt in ea.
paras.en: But according to Gregory, some are so simple that they do not know what is right; and they forsake the innocence of true simplicity by the very fact that they do not rise to the virtue of uprightness. For this reason Paul says: [[Rom 16:19|I would have you to be wise in good and simple in evil|Volo vos sapientes esse in bono, simplices autem in malo]]. And Christ himself: [[Matt 10:16|Be ye therefore wise as serpents and simple as doves|Estote prudentes sicut serpentes, et simplices sicut columbæ]]: that is, that the serpent's cunning might instruct the dove's simplicity, and the dove's simplicity temper the serpent's cunning. Hence the Holy Ghost appeared not only in the form of a dove[[Matt 3:16||]] but also in fire[[Acts 2:3||]]. For by the dove simplicity is expressed, by the fire zeal. And those who are filled with the Holy Ghost so devote themselves to the meekness of simplicity that they are also kindled with the zeal of uprightness against the faults of wrongdoers. Hence Solomon too joins these two, saying: [[Prov 2:21|they that are upright, shall dwell in the earth; and the simple shall continue in it|Qui recti sunt, habitabunt in terra, et simplices permanebunt in ea]].

paras.t: Ac timens Deum, timore filiali, reverentiali et casto, qui ex sincero Dei amore producitur, vel timore illo, qui unum de septem donis vocatur. Hic timor ad omne bonum sollicitat, quum sit fuga mali culpæ, seu abominatio offensæ Dei, quem quo serenius ardentiusque amamus, eo ipsius inhonorationem diligentius evitamus. Ideo in Proverbiis scriptum est: Timor Domini fons vitæ, ut declinet a ruina mortis. Et denuo Salomon ait: Qui timet Deum, nihil negligit. Ideo dicit Gregorius: Deum timere, est nulla quæ facienda sunt præterire. Quomodo autem sanctus Job Deum timuerit, ipse infra fatetur: Semper, inquiens, quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum. O quam beatus est cui datum est sic timere Deum!
paras.en: [[1:1|and fearing God|Ac timens Deum]], with a filial fear, reverent and chaste, which springs from a sincere love of God; or with that fear which is called one of the seven gifts[[Is 11:3||]]. This fear spurs one on to every good, since it is a flight from the evil of sin, or a loathing of offending God: the more serenely and ardently we love him, the more carefully we avoid dishonouring him. Therefore it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 14:27|The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life, to decline from the ruin of death|Timor Domini fons vitæ, ut declinet a ruina mortis]]. And again Solomon says: [[Eccles 7:19|he that feareth God, neglecteth nothing|Qui timet Deum, nihil negligit]]. Therefore Gregory says: To fear God is to pass over nothing that ought to be done. How holy Job feared God he himself confesses below, saying: [[Job 31:23|I have always feared God as waves swelling over me|Semper, inquiens, quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum]]. O how blessed is he to whom it is given so to fear God[[Ecclus 34:17||]]!

paras.t: Et recedens a malo, peccata vitando. Peccatum enim est fugibilitatis infinitæ, quum sit aversio a bono immenso, infinitæque majestatis Dei offensio. Ideo scriptum est: Quasi a facie colubri fuge peccata. Duæ autem sunt partes justitiæ, quas tangit Psalmista, dicendo: Declina a malo: ad quod pertinent præcepta negativa, quæ obligant semper et ad semper; et fac bonum: ad quod pertinent præcepta affirmativa, quæ obligant semper, sed non ad semper. Receditur autem a malo culpæ per mentis dissensum; interdum quoque et corpore recedendum a malo, ut a choreis atque spectaculis. Dicit hoc loco Gregorius: Neque bona opera Deo accepta sunt, quæ ante ejus oculos malorum admixtione maculantur. Hinc namque Salomon ait: Qui in uno offenderit, multa bona perdet. Et Jacobus: Quicumque totam legem servaverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus. Paulus quoque: Modicum, inquit, fermentum totam massam corrumpit. Verumtamen totum hoc de admixtione mortalis peccati sumendum est. Alioqui nonne, Isaia testante, quasi pannus menstruatæ sunt universæ justitiæ nostræ?
paras.en: [[1:1|and avoiding evil|Et recedens a malo]], by shunning sins. For sin is infinitely to be fled from, since it is a turning away from the boundless good and an offence against the infinite majesty of God. Therefore it is written: [[Ecclus 21:2|Flee from sins as from the face of a serpent|Quasi a facie colubri fuge peccata]]. Now there are two parts of justice, which the Psalmist touches on when he says: [[Ps 36:27|Decline from evil|Declina a malo]], to which belong the negative precepts, which bind always and at every moment; [[Ps 36:27|and do good|et fac bonum]], to which belong the affirmative precepts, which bind always, but not at every moment [*semper et ad semper*: a negative precept, such as “thou shalt not steal”, may be broken at no moment; an affirmative one, such as to pray, binds always, but is to be fulfilled at its proper times]. One withdraws from the evil of sin by the mind's refusal; but at times one must also withdraw from evil with the body, as from dances and shows. Gregory says on this place: Nor are good works acceptable to God which before his eyes are stained by an admixture of evil deeds. Hence Solomon says: [[Eccles 9:18|he that shall offend in one, shall lose many good things|Qui in uno offenderit, multa bona perdet]]. And James: [[Jas 2:10|whosoever shall keep the whole law, but offend in one point, is become guilty of all|Quicumque totam legem servaverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus]]. Paul too: [[1 Cor 5:6|a little|Modicum]], he says, [[1 Cor 5:6|leaven corrupteth the whole lump|fermentum totam massam corrumpit]][[Gal 5:9||]]. All this, however, is to be understood of an admixture of mortal sin. Otherwise, as Isaias testifies, are not [[Is 64:6|all our justices as the rag of a menstruous woman|quasi pannus menstruatæ sunt universæ justitiæ nostræ]]?

paras.t: Ex præhabitis patet, quod Job bene habuerit se ad Deum, ad proximum et ad se ipsum. Ut enim Thomas hic scribit, tripliciter peccat homo, scilicet in Deum, in proximum, in se ipsum. In proximum autem dupliciter, scilicet occulte per fraudulentiam, et aperte per violentiam. Job autem proximum dolo non circumvenit: nam dicitur, Erat vir simplex. Nec vi oppressit: nam subditur, Et rectus. Quod vero non peccavit in Deum, monstratur dum jungitur, Ac timens Deum. Nec in se ipsum: nam sequitur, Et recedens a malo. Malum enim odio habuit propter se, utpote quia malum, non solum propter nocumentum hominis offensamque Dei. Quomodo autem Job dicatur nec verbo nec facto peccasse, infra discutiemus.
paras.en: From what has been said it is clear that Job conducted himself well towards God, towards his neighbour and towards himself. For, as Thomas writes here, man sins in three ways: against God, against his neighbour, and against himself. And against his neighbour in two ways: secretly, by fraud, and openly, by violence. But Job did not get the better of his neighbour by guile, for it is said: [[1:1|that man was simple|Erat vir simplex]]. Nor did he oppress him by force, for there follows: [[1:1|and upright|Et rectus]]. That he did not sin against God is shown where there is added: [[1:1|and fearing God|Ac timens Deum]]. Nor against himself, for there follows: [[1:1|and avoiding evil|Et recedens a malo]]. For he hated evil for its own sake, as being evil, and not only for the harm it does to man and the offence it gives to God. How Job is said to have sinned neither in word nor in deed we shall discuss below.

paras.t: Hucusque ostensum est, qualis fuit Job in bono monastico, quod est bonum personæ. Deinde describitur qualis fuit in bono œconomico, id est domestico. Natique sunt ei septem filii, et tres filiæ.
