Primo beati Job prosperitas notificatur, ut ex hoc magnitudo suæ adversitatis clarius insinuetur: opposita enim juxta se posita, lucidius innotescunt; simul etiam ad ostendendum (ut Thomas affirmat) quod ex prima Dei intentione justis semper bona præstantur, non spiritualia tantum, sed corporalia quoque ac temporalia. Sed quod aliquando justi adversitatibus affliguntur, ob specialem aliquam accidit causam. Unde et a principio sic institutus est homo, ut nullis subjaceret adversitatibus, si in innocentia permansisset. Principium autem temporalis prosperitatis, post bonam propriæ personæ consistentiam, consistit in personis conjunctis, præsertim in sobole. Proles enim est quasi aliquid suorum parentum, secundum illud Ecclesiastici: Mortuus est pater ejus, et quasi non est mortuus; reliquit enim similem sibi filium. Ideo fecunditas prolis beati Job explicatur. Idque ad prosperitatis augmentum pertinuit, quod filii plures erant quam filiæ. Sexus namque masculinus perfectior est, et filii magis consueverunt optari quam filiæ: propter quod dicit Augustinus super Joannem, quod majus est gaudium dum nascitur filius quam puella. Filii quoque efficaciores sunt ad domus aliarumque rerum dispositionem ac regimen. Nam corpore rationisque usu fortiores solent exsistere. Præterea (sicut Gregorius ait) sæpe ad avaritiam corda parentum trahit fecunditas prolis. Nam tanto plus ad congregandas divitias inflammantur, quo pluribus heredibus fecundantur. Hoc ergo ad sancti Job spectat præconium, quod tot natis abundavit, nec tamen ab æquitate per temporalium amorem superfluum declinavit.
paras.en: Thus far it has been shown what Job was in monastic good, which is the good of the person [in the scholastic division of moral philosophy, *monastica* is the ethics of the single person, as *œconomica* is that of the household and *politica* that of the city]. Next it is described what he was in economic good, that is, in the good of the household. [[1:2|And there were born to him seven sons and three daughters|Natique sunt ei septem filii, et tres filiæ]]. First blessed Job's prosperity is made known, so that the greatness of his adversity may be shown the more clearly by it: for opposites set side by side are more plainly seen. At the same time it serves to show (as Thomas affirms) that by God's first intention good things are always given to the just, not spiritual only, but bodily and temporal too; and that when the just are at times afflicted with adversities, this happens for some special cause. Hence too man was so made from the beginning that he would have been subject to no adversities, had he remained in innocence. Now the beginning of temporal prosperity, after the good standing of one's own person, lies in the persons joined to one, above all in one's offspring. For offspring is as it were something of its parents, according to that word of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 30:4|His father is dead, and he is as if he were not dead: for he hath left one behind him that is like himself|Mortuus est pater ejus, et quasi non est mortuus; reliquit enim similem sibi filium]]. Therefore the fruitfulness of blessed Job in offspring is set out. And it added to his prosperity that the sons were more than the daughters. For the male sex is the more perfect, and sons are more commonly wished for than daughters: for which reason Augustine says on John that there is greater joy when a son is born than a girl. Sons are also more able in ordering and ruling a household and other affairs, since they are usually stronger in body and in the use of reason. Moreover (as Gregory says), the fruitfulness of offspring often draws the hearts of parents to avarice; for they are the more inflamed to heap up riches, the more heirs they are blessed with. This, then, belongs to the praise of holy Job: that he abounded in so many children, and yet did not turn aside from equity through an excessive love of temporal things.

paras.t: Et fuit possessio ejus. Possessio dicitur quasi pedum positio, quia ad nutum habetur, et possidenti subjicitur, non dominatur. Septem millia ovium. Ovis (secundum Albertum) est animal mansuetum, simplex, valdeque utile, fimo, lacte, carne, cibo, pelle, calceamento, lana, intestinis et vestimento. Et tria millia camelorum, qui utiles sunt ad onera deferenda; quingenta quoque juga boum, qui faciunt mille boves, qui ad terras colendas deserviunt, et multipliciter utiles sunt; et quingentæ asinæ, ac familia multa nimis, quæ ad tot animalium pastum atque custodiam necessaria fuit. Ideo autem opulentia Job per jumenta describitur, quia possessio animalium pretiosior antiquitus fuit quam agrorum; imo animalia fuerunt præcipue antiquorum divitiæ: agri enim propter hominum paucitatem plus abundabant, et maxime in partibus orientis, in quibus usque hodie sunt pauci habitatores præ latitudine regionis, ut scribit hic Thomas.
paras.en: [[1:3|And his possession was|Et fuit possessio ejus]]. *Possessio*, possession, is so called as if *pedum positio*, “a placing of the feet”, because it is had at one's beck, and is subject to the possessor, not his master. [[1:3|seven thousand sheep|Septem millia ovium]]. The sheep (according to Albert) is a gentle animal, simple, and very useful: by its dung, its milk, its flesh for food, its skin for shoes, its wool, its entrails, and for clothing. [[1:3|and three thousand camels|Et tria millia camelorum]], which are useful for carrying loads; [[1:3|five hundred yoke of oxen|quingenta quoque juga boum]], which make a thousand oxen, which serve for tilling the land and are useful in many ways; [[1:3|and five hundred she asses|et quingentæ asinæ]], [[1:3|and a family exceedingly great|ac familia multa nimis]], which was needed to feed and keep so many animals. Job's wealth is described by his beasts because in ancient times a possession of animals was more precious than one of fields; indeed animals were the chief riches of the ancients: for fields were more plentiful because men were few, most of all in the parts of the east, where to this day there are few inhabitants for the breadth of the country, as Thomas writes here.

paras.t: Porro (secundum Philosophum) quatuor virtutibus regitur domus: quarum prima est uxoraria, quæ est scientia et virtus bene utendi uxore; secunda est paterna, quæ senatoria dicitur; tertia chrimatistica seu thesauritiva; quarta despotica, quæ est virtus bene utendi servis atque ancillis. Harum nulla defuit Job. Prima notatur, quum dicitur, Nati sunt ei, videlicet ex uxore legitima, quæ se habet in domo sicut regina in regno. Secunda notatur ibi, Septem filii, etc. Tertia ibi, Fuit possessio ejus. Quarta autem, quum sequitur, Ac familia multa nimis. Convenienter demum scribitur Job possedisse tam multa, ut magnitudo patientiæ perfectionisque suæ clarius innotescat, dum omnia illa sine impatientia amisisse narratur. Majorem namque dolorem inferunt damna majora; et nunquam sine dolore amittitur, nisi quod sine amore superfluo possidetur. Magnæ ergo fuit virtutis, tot opes sine inordinato possidere affectu, nec per eas a mentis stabilitate atque custodia impediri.
paras.en: Now (according to the Philosopher) a household is ruled by four virtues. The first of them is the conjugal, which is the knowledge and virtue of dealing rightly with a wife; the second is the paternal, which is called senatorial; the third the chrematistic, or treasure-gathering [*chrimatistica*, from the Greek: the art of getting and keeping wealth]; the fourth the despotic, which is the virtue of dealing rightly with menservants and maidservants. None of these was wanting in Job. The first is marked when it is said, [[1:2|there were born to him|Nati sunt ei]], namely from a lawful wife, who stands in the house as a queen in the kingdom. The second is marked at [[1:2|seven sons|Septem filii]], etc. The third at [[1:3|his possession was|Fuit possessio ejus]]. And the fourth where there follows, [[1:3|and a family exceedingly great|Ac familia multa nimis]]. Lastly, it is fittingly written that Job possessed so much, so that the greatness of his patience and perfection may be the more clearly known when he is related to have lost all of it without impatience. For greater losses bring greater grief; and nothing is ever lost without grief except what is possessed without excessive love. It was therefore a mark of great virtue to possess so much wealth without inordinate affection, and not to be hindered by it in the steadiness and watchfulness of the mind.

paras.t: Denique triplex est bonum, scilicet bonum hominis, quod est bonum simpliciter; bonum domus, quod est melius; et bonum civitatis ac gentis seu patriæ, quod primo Ethicorum optimum divinissimumque vocatur. Hinc subditur, qualis fuerit Job in bono hoc tertio. Eratque vir ille magnus, bonitate, sapientia, fama, honore et gloria, inter omnes orientales, qui prædivites sunt, secundum Gregorium: et in hoc prosperitas ejus terrena perficiebatur, quod etiam fama inclytus fuit. Nam in Ecclesiaste scriptum est: Melius est nomen bonum quam unguenta pretiosa. Et alibi: Curam habe de bono nomine, hoc enim magis proderit tibi quam thesauri.
paras.en: Lastly, good is threefold: the good of a man, which is good simply; the good of a household, which is better; and the good of a city and nation or fatherland, which in the first book of the Ethics is called the best and most divine. Hence there follows what Job was in this third good: [[1:3|and this man was great|Eratque vir ille magnus]] in goodness, wisdom, fame, honour and glory, [[1:3|among all the people of the east|inter omnes orientales]], who are very rich, according to Gregory. And in this his earthly prosperity was made complete, that he was also renowned in fame. For it is written in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 7:2|A good name is better than precious ointments|Melius est nomen bonum quam unguenta pretiosa]]. And elsewhere: [[Ecclus 41:15|Take care of a good name: for this shall continue with thee, more than a thousand treasures|Curam habe de bono nomine, hoc enim magis proderit tibi quam thesauri]] [Denis's wording here is “for this will profit thee more than treasures”].

paras.t: Et ibant filii ejus sex, ad domum illius in qua fuerant comesturi, qui septimus fuit; et faciebant convivia, id est, pariter vescebantur, per domos, id est successive in domo uniuscujusque ipsorum, unusquisque in die suo: ita quod quolibet die simul edebant, primo die hebdomadæ incipientes comedere in domo primogeniti, ut apparet, et deinde secundum ordinem dierum hebdomadæ et nativitatis filiorum, comedebant in domibus ceteris successive: sicque completa hebdomada, complebatur convescentia in domibus singulorum; et sequentis hebdomadæ prima die reincipiebatur in domo fratris senioris. Ex quo sequitur, quod inter fratres istos fuit grandis stabilisque concordia, frugaliterque vixerunt: quorum utrumque ad laudem pertinet patris eorum, qui eos taliter rexit, quum tamen opulentiam rerum frequenter sequatur discordia atque tenacitas. Et mittentes vocabant tres sorores suas, invitando eas per nuntium, ut comederent et biberent cum eis. In quo insinuatur, quod non instar quorumdam protervorum ac superborum fratrum, sorores suas despexerant ob sexus inferioritatem, imo honorem eis tanquam infirmiori vasculo impendebant, prout a patre suo edocti erant. Hinc dicit Gregorius: O inæstimabilem paternæ institutionis laudem! Et pater dives dicitur, et filii concordes asseruntur; et dum dividenda inter eos substantia aderat, corda tamen omnium caritas indivisa implebat.
paras.en: [[1:4|And his sons went|Et ibant filii ejus]], six of them, to the house of the one at whose house they were to eat, who made the seventh; [[1:4|and made a feast|et faciebant convivia]], that is, they ate together, [[1:4|by houses|per domos]], that is, in turn in the house of each of them, [[1:4|every one in his day|unusquisque in die suo]]: so that each day they ate together, beginning on the first day of the week in the house of the firstborn, as it appears, and then, following the order of the days of the week and of the sons' births, eating in the other houses in turn; and so, when the week was complete, the round of their meals in the house of each was complete, and on the first day of the following week it began again in the house of the eldest brother. From this it follows that among these brothers there was a great and lasting concord, and that they lived soberly: both of which redound to the praise of their father, who ruled them so, though discord and tight-fistedness often follow on abundance of wealth. [[1:4|And sending, they called their three sisters|Et mittentes vocabant tres sorores suas]], inviting them by a messenger, [[1:4|to eat and drink with them|ut comederent et biberent cum eis]]. In this it is suggested that, unlike certain wanton and proud brothers, they did not despise their sisters for the weakness of their sex, but rather paid them honour [[1 Pet 3:7|as to the weaker vessel|tanquam infirmiori vasculo]], as they had been taught by their father. Hence Gregory says: O inestimable praise of a father's training! The father is said to be rich, and the sons are declared to be of one mind; and while there was property to be divided among them, an undivided charity yet filled the hearts of all.

paras.t: Cumque in orbem, id est circulum hebdomadæ, transissent dies convivii, redeundo ab ultimo ac minore ad primum, utpote die octava secundum Gregorium, septem scilicet diebus hebdomadæ evolutis, mittebat ad eos Job nuntium quemdam, vel sacerdotem, secundum Albertum; et sanctificabat illos: maculis, quas convivantes incurrere solent, instrumentaliter, quantum potuit, expurgavit eos, per internuntium seu epistolam exhortando ad diluenda mala præterita, ac futura vitanda; vel forte per aliquem ritum oblationis seu expiationis eos sanctificavit. Sacrificia namque et primitiarum ac decimarum oblatio, ante legem scriptam fuerunt, prout Hugo in libro de Sacramentis plenius docet. Consurgensque diluculo, implens illud Ecclesiastici, Justus cor suum tradet ad vigilandum diluculo ad Dominum; itemque illud Psalmistæ, Mane adstabo tibi et videbo. Hac equidem hora sensibus sobriis consistentibus, et mente exterioribus negotiis nondum involuta, aptior est ad devotionem homo. Ideo dicit Salvator: Primo quærite regnum Dei. Et Isaias Deum orsus affari: De mane, inquit, vigilabo ad te. Offerebat holocausta per singulos, id est, pro quolibet obtulit speciale holocaustum, septem videlicet holocausta, secundum Albertum et Thomam. Ex quo videtur, quod pro filiabus non obtulit: vel quia noverat eas tam verecundas ac virtuosas, quod de earum excessu notabili non timebat; vel forte etiam pro eis obtulit, quamvis non exprimatur, sed nomine filiorum etiam filiæ intelliguntur: quemadmodum infra in isto capitulo, domus cadens dicitur oppressisse liberos, id est filios Job, nec dubium quin filias quoque ejus oppresserit, quamvis non exprimatur. Porro holocaustum fuit solennius sacrificium, quoniam ad divinæ reverentiam majestatis totum comburebatur, nulla ejus parte ad offerentium usum manente.
paras.en: [[1:5|And when|Cumque]] in the round [*in orbem*, which the Douay-Rheims renders “gone about”], that is, the circle of the week, [[1:5|the days of their feasting were gone about|transissent dies convivii]], returning from the last and youngest to the first: that is, on the eighth day according to Gregory, once the seven days of the week had run their course, [[1:5|Job sent to them|mittebat ad eos Job]] a messenger, or a priest according to Albert; [[1:5|and sanctified them|et sanctificabat illos]]: that is, he cleansed them, as an instrument and as far as he could, of the stains that those who feast are wont to contract, by exhorting them through a go-between or a letter to wash away past evils and shun future ones; or perhaps he sanctified them by some rite of offering or expiation. For sacrifices, and the offering of firstfruits and tithes, existed before the written law, as Hugh teaches more fully in his book On the Sacraments. [[1:5|and rising up early|Consurgensque diluculo]], fulfilling that word of Ecclesiasticus, The just man [[Ecclus 39:6|will give his heart to resort early to the Lord|cor suum tradet ad vigilandum diluculo ad Dominum]]; and also that of the Psalmist, [[Ps 5:5|In the morning I will stand before thee, and I will see|Mane adstabo tibi et videbo]]. For at this hour, when the senses are sober and the mind is not yet entangled in outward business, a man is more apt for devotion. Therefore the Saviour says: [[Matt 6:33|Seek ye therefore first the kingdom of God|Primo quærite regnum Dei]]. And Isaias, beginning to speak to God: [[Is 26:9|in the morning early|De mane]], he says, [[Is 26:9|I will watch to thee|vigilabo ad te]]. [[1:5|offered holocausts for every one of them|Offerebat holocausta per singulos]], that is, for each one he offered a holocaust of his own, namely seven holocausts, according to Albert and Thomas. From this it seems that he did not offer for the daughters: either because he knew them to be so modest and virtuous that he feared no notable excess on their part; or perhaps he offered for them too, though it is not expressed, and under the name of sons the daughters too are understood: just as below in this chapter the falling house is said to have crushed the children[[1:19||]], that is, Job's sons, and there is no doubt that it crushed his daughters too, though this is not expressed. Now the holocaust was the more solemn sacrifice, since it was burnt whole in reverence of the divine majesty, no part of it being left for the use of those who offered it.

paras.t: Dicebat enim, tanquam de filiorum salute sollicitus, magis autem pro Dei honoratione accensus: Ne forte peccaverint filii mei. Sobrie circumspecteque loquitur, docens temerarium judicium esse vitandum. Ideo de actibus absentium atque incertis assertive non loquitur, quamvis probabiliter noverit eos in quotidianis conviviis non penitus caruisse peccatis, venialibus saltem. Convivantes namque solent multipliciter excedere, scilicet in quantitate, in delectatione, in loquacitate, in risu, in cordis quoque inepta lætitia. Ideo homo timoratus debet cum magna cordis custodia sumere cibum ac potum, præsertim quando cum aliis vescitur vel delicatioribus utitur.
paras.en: [[1:5|For he said|Dicebat enim]], as one anxious for his sons' salvation, but still more kindled for the honour of God: [[1:5|Lest perhaps my sons have sinned|Ne forte peccaverint filii mei]]. He speaks soberly and with caution, teaching that rash judgment is to be avoided. So he does not speak with assurance of the acts of those who are absent and of things uncertain, although he knew it to be likely that in their daily feasts they had not been wholly without sins, venial ones at least. For those who feast are wont to go too far in many ways: in quantity, in pleasure, in talk, in laughter, and also in unseemly mirth of heart. Therefore a God-fearing man ought to take food and drink with great guard over his heart, especially when he eats with others or takes daintier fare.

paras.t: Et benedixerint Deo in cordibus suis, id est, cogitando maledixerint Deo. Sed quum maledicere Deo, sit gravissimum scelus, mirum quod tantum facinus suspicabatur de filiis suis, quos tanta disciplina compescuit et tam probos cognovit; imo dicit Gregorius: Beati Job filii tanta fuerant bonæ institutionis disciplina accincti, ut neque per facta in conviviis, neque per verba delinquerent: perfectos quippe eos esse in opere et sermone docuerat. Ad quod respondendum videtur, quod non putavit eos in verba maledictionis prorupisse, nec tentationi de maledicendo Deo plenarie consensisse; sed timuit ne circa hoc habuerint aliquem primum motum vel cogitationem incautam. Quoniam enim inter gentiles atque idololatras habitabant, poterant aliquando tentari de inhonoratione Dei præfata, videndo prosperitates servientium idolis. Hinc dicit Gregorius, quod Job de sola cogitatione pro suis filiis metuebat. Præallegatum quoque verbum Gregorii de perfectione filiorum Job, sumendum est quod a mortalibus abstinere solebant excessibus; et si quid tale incurrerant, mox emendare curabant.
paras.en: [[1:5|and have blessed God in their hearts|Et benedixerint Deo in cordibus suis]], that is, have cursed God in thought. But since to curse God is a most grievous crime, it is strange that he suspected so great a wickedness of his sons, whom he had kept in check with such discipline and knew to be so upright; indeed Gregory says: The sons of blessed Job were girt with such discipline of good training that they offended neither by deeds nor by words in their feasts: for he had taught them to be perfect in deed and in speech. To this, it seems, we must answer that he did not think they had broken out into words of cursing, nor fully consented to a temptation to curse God; but he feared lest they had had some first movement or unguarded thought about it [a first movement (*primus motus*) is a stirring of the soul that comes before reason can deliberate, and is at most a venial sin]. For since they lived among Gentiles and idolaters, they could at times be tempted to the dishonouring of God just mentioned, on seeing the prosperity of those who served idols. Hence Gregory says that Job feared for his sons on account of thought alone. And the saying of Gregory quoted above about the perfection of Job's sons is to be taken to mean that they were wont to keep from mortal excesses, and if they fell into any such thing, they took care to amend it at once.

paras.t: Denique, in Scripturis frequenter maledictio Dei, per ejus benedictionem per antiphrasim designatur, sicut et infra statim patebit, eo quod tantus sit horror hujus peccati, quod est blasphemare seu maledicere Deo, quod pia ora ipsum proprio nomine exprimere horrent, sed per contrarium suum illud designant. Verumtamen Thomas tangit modum, quo benedictio possit hic accipi sicut sonat, ut scilicet totum istud, Ne forte peccaverint filii mei et benedixerint Deo in cordibus suis, accipiatur conjunctim: eritque sensus, Ne forte peccaverint, et de ipsis actibus vitiosis benedixerint Deo, quasi complaceant Deo peccata, sicut latrones atque prædones prædam sortiti, Deo sæpe gratias referunt. Quamvis autem benedicere Deo, secundum se sit bonum, tamen sic benedicere Deo, est malum, significatque voluntatem in vitiis quiescentem. Unde sic vituperatur, dum apud Zachariam dicitur contra quosdam pascentes pecora occisionis: Quæ qui possederant, occidebant, et non dolebant, dicentes, Benedictus Dominus, divites facti sumus.
paras.en: Further, in the Scriptures the cursing of God is often signified by his blessing, by antiphrasis [that is, by saying the opposite of what is meant], as will also be plain just below: because the horror of this sin, that is, of blaspheming or cursing God, is so great that pious lips shrink from expressing it by its own name, and signify it by its contrary. Thomas, however, touches on a way in which *blessing* may here be taken as it sounds: namely, that the whole of this, [[1:5|Lest perhaps my sons have sinned, and have blessed God in their hearts|Ne forte peccaverint filii mei et benedixerint Deo in cordibus suis]], be taken together; and the sense will be: Lest perhaps they have sinned, and have blessed God for those very sinful acts, as though sins were pleasing to God, as thieves and robbers, when they have got their booty, often give thanks to God. For though to bless God is good in itself, yet so to bless God is evil, and signifies a will at rest in vice. Hence it is rebuked in Zacharias, where it is said against certain men who fed the flock of slaughter: [[Zach 11:5|Which they that possessed, slew, and repented not|Quæ qui possederant, occidebant, et non dolebant]], [[Zach 11:5|saying: Blessed be the Lord, we are become rich|dicentes, Benedictus Dominus, divites facti sumus]].

paras.t: Sic faciebat Job cunctis diebus, id est quolibet die octavo secundum modum præhabitum, utpote circulo conviviorum per hebdomadam jam completo. Sciebat enim quod postea locutus est Christus: Qui perseveraverit usque in finem, hic salvus erit. Multi enim ferventer incipiunt, sed paulatim tepescunt, vel omnino omittunt, similes illis quibus ad Galatas ait Apostolus: Sic stulti estis, ut quum spiritu cœperitis, nunc carne consummemini? Denique opus Dei a quibusdam devote peragitur, si sit rarum; si vero sit frequens, minus attenditur, aut in fastidium vertitur: quod negligentiæ est sive acediæ, dum quis de spirituali tædiatur labore. Talem vero non fuisse beatum Job, inducta verba testantur. Nos ergo opus Dei tanto agamus vigilantius atque ardentius, quanto frequentius. Maledictus enim qui facit opus Dei negligenter. Sicque perseveremus in bono cunctis diebus. Ad hoc enim incarnatus est venitque Filius Dei, ut sine timore de manu inimicorum nostrorum liberati, serviamus illi in sanctitate et justitia coram ipso, omnibus diebus vitæ nostræ.
paras.en: [[1:5|So did Job all days|Sic faciebat Job cunctis diebus]], that is, on every eighth day in the manner described above, the round of feasts having by then been completed through the week. For he knew what Christ said afterwards: [[Matt 10:22|he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved|Qui perseveraverit usque in finem, hic salvus erit]]. For many begin fervently, but little by little grow lukewarm, or give up altogether, like those to whom the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Galatians: [[Gal 3:3|Are you so foolish that, whereas you began in the Spirit, you would now be made perfect by the flesh?|Sic stulti estis, ut quum spiritu cœperitis, nunc carne consummemini?]] Again, the work of God is carried out devoutly by some if it is rare; but if it is frequent, it is attended to less, or turns to weariness: which belongs to negligence or to acedia [that is, spiritual sloth: a sadness and weariness about spiritual good], when one grows weary of spiritual labour. But the words brought in here bear witness that blessed Job was not such a man. Let us, then, do the work of God the more watchfully and ardently, the more often we do it. For [[Jer 48:10|Cursed be he that doth the work of|Maledictus enim qui facit opus]] God negligently [Denis reads *opus Dei negligenter*, the work of God negligently, where the Vulgate has *opus Domini fraudulenter*, the work of the Lord deceitfully]. And so let us persevere in good all days. For to this end the Son of God became incarnate and came, that [[Luke 1:74|being delivered from the hand of our enemies, we may serve him without fear|sine timore de manu inimicorum nostrorum liberati, serviamus illi]] [[Luke 1:75|in holiness and justice before him|in sanctitate et justitia coram ipso]], all the days of our life.

paras.t: Ex præhabitis claret, quantam sollicitudinem habuit sanctus Job pro filiis suis, ne Deum offenderent: quem parentes imitari tenentur, filios ac filias instruendo, a malis retrahendo, ad bona inducendo. Parentes quippe (ut etiam Philosophus loquitur) filiis tenentur educationem, instructionem et disciplinam seu correctionem. Unde ad Ephesios dicit Apostolus: Patres, educate filios vestros in disciplina et correptione Domini. Insuper patet ex dictis, quod licet Job filiis suis convivia ista admisit, ipse tamen in suo rigore, parsimonia et gravitate permansit, vitans convivia. Juniori enim ætati aliqua rationabiliter permittuntur, quæ seniores non decent. Et forte filios suos ac filias maluit pariter convivari, quam aliorum comessationibus commisceri, sciens suorum probitatem, et ne aliorum vitiis inficerentur.
paras.en: From what has been said it is clear how great a care holy Job had for his sons, lest they should offend God: and parents are bound to imitate him, by instructing their sons and daughters, drawing them back from evil and leading them on to good. For parents (as the Philosopher [that is, Aristotle] also says) owe their children upbringing, instruction, and discipline or correction. Hence the Apostle says to the Ephesians: [[Eph 6:4|fathers|Patres]], [[Eph 6:4|bring them up in the discipline and correction of the Lord|educate filios vestros in disciplina et correptione Domini]] [Denis has *educate filios vestros*, bring up your children]. Moreover it is plain from what has been said that, although Job allowed his sons these feasts, he himself kept to his strictness, frugality and gravity, avoiding feasts. For some things are reasonably permitted to a younger age which do not become older men. And perhaps he preferred that his sons and daughters should feast together rather than mix in the revels of others, knowing the uprightness of his own, and lest they should be infected with the vices of others.

paras.t: Consequenter processus tentationis atque adversitas Job recitantur. Quadam autem die, quum venissent filii Dei ut adsisterent coram Domino, adfuit inter eos etiam Satan. Quamvis absolute loquendo, omnes angeli sancti Deo ministrent laude continua, atque adsistant contemplatione perpetua, quum dicat Apostolus, Omnes sunt administratorii spiritus; et Psalmista, Benedicite Domino, omnes virtutes ejus, ministri ejus, qui facitis voluntatem ejus; itemque Salvator, Angeli eorum in cœlis semper vident faciem Patris mei: per appropriationem tamen ministrare dicuntur, qui ad explenda foris ministeria divinitus emittuntur; adsistere vero, qui sic intimæ Dei visione fruuntur, quod foris nequaquam mittuntur. Sicque in Daniele legitur: Millia millium ministrabant ei, et decies millies centena millia adsistebant ei. Sed iste modus adsistendi Deo propriissimus appellatur, non nisi superioribus angelorum ordinibus competens. Alio igitur modo adsistere Deo extensius sumitur, ut sit idem quod vultui gloriæ ejus intendere, totaque mente ad omne beneplacitum ejus promptum consistere: et sic universis angelorum competit choris. Unde tertio Regum ait Michæas propheta: Vidi Dominum sedentem super solium suum, et omnem exercitum cœli adsistentem ei a dextris et a sinistris. Tertio autem adsistere Deo communissime sumitur, ut sit idem quod divinæ præsentiæ cognitum esse, sicut Apostolus ait, Omnia nuda et aperta sunt oculis ejus: sicque omnibus competit creaturis.
paras.en: Next are related the course of Job's temptation and his adversity. [[1:6|Now on a certain day, when the sons of God came to stand before the Lord, Satan also was present among them|Quadam autem die, quum venissent filii Dei ut adsisterent coram Domino, adfuit inter eos etiam Satan]]. Absolutely speaking, all the holy angels minister to God with continual praise, and stand before Him in perpetual contemplation, since the Apostle says, They are [[Heb 1:14|all ministering spirits|Omnes sunt administratorii spiritus]]; and the Psalmist, [[Ps 102:21|Bless the Lord, all ye his hosts: you ministers of his that do his will|Benedicite Domino, omnes virtutes ejus, ministri ejus, qui facitis voluntatem ejus]]; and likewise the Saviour, [[Matt 18:10|their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father|Angeli eorum in cœlis semper vident faciem Patris mei]]: yet by appropriation [that is, by applying the word more particularly to some of them] those are said to minister who are sent forth by God to fulfil ministries outside; and those to stand before Him who so enjoy the inmost vision of God that they are never sent outside. And so we read in Daniel: [[Dan 7:10|thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him|Millia millium ministrabant ei, et decies millies centena millia adsistebant ei]]. But this way of standing before God is called the most proper, and belongs only to the higher orders of angels. In another way, then, to stand before God is taken more broadly, so as to be the same as to attend to the face of His glory, and to stand ready with the whole mind for His every good pleasure: and in this sense it belongs to all the choirs of angels. Hence in the third book of Kings Micheas the prophet says: [[3 Kings 22:19|I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the army of heaven standing by him on the right hand and on the left|Vidi Dominum sedentem super solium suum, et omnem exercitum cœli adsistentem ei a dextris et a sinistris]]. Thirdly, to stand before God is taken most commonly, so as to be the same as to be known to the divine presence, as the Apostle says, [[Heb 4:13|all things are naked and open to his eyes|Omnia nuda et aperta sunt oculis ejus]]: and in this sense it belongs to all creatures.

paras.t: Præterea advertendum, quod angeli sancti deputantur custodiæ hominum, sicut et dæmones ad tentandum et exercitandum hominibus deputantur. Itaque angeli sancti sæpe de cœlis destinantur ad viatores ad succursum eorum, rursusque redeunt ad superna: et hoc fit certis temporibus, quamvis motus et operatio angelorum non mensurentur tempore, quod ponitur species quantitatis. Sic ergo nunc dicitur: Quadam die, quum venissent filii Dei, id est angeli sancti animarum custodes, de ipsis hominibus circa quos operati fuerunt, quibus et realiter adfuerunt. Sunt namque angeli in loco definitive, et ubi operantur, ibi esse dicuntur; expletoque ministerio, propter quod descenderunt, mox ad cœlestia revertuntur. Hinc namque Daniel ait: Adhuc me loquente in oratione mea, ecce Gabriel cito volans tetigit me et docuit me. Dixitque Gabriel: Nunc egressus sum ut docerem te et intelligeres. Ego autem veni ut indicarem tibi. Sic et in Judicum libro habetur: Angelus Domini ascendit de Galgala ad locum Flentium. Itemque: Quum ascenderet flamma altaris in cœlum, angelus Domini pariter in flamma ascendit. Insuper, Tobiæ Raphael angelus ait: Tempus est ut revertar ad eum qui me misit. Et Zacharias propheta attestatur: Ecce angelus qui loquebatur in me, egrediebatur, et alius angelus egrediebatur in occursum ejus, et dixit: Curre, et loquere ad puerum istum. Ex quibus omnibus multisque aliis Scripturæ locis patescit, quod angeli sancti moventur de loco ad locum, veniuntque de cœlo ad homines, et revertuntur ad cœlos horis atque temporibus a Deo præordinatis.
paras.en: It is to be noted, moreover, that the holy angels are appointed to the guardianship of men, as the demons too are appointed to tempt and exercise men. And so the holy angels are often dispatched from heaven to wayfarers [that is, men still on the way, in this life] to help them, and go back again to the heights: and this happens at fixed times, though the motion and working of the angels are not measured by time, which is reckoned a species of quantity. So, then, it is now said: [[1:6|on a certain day, when the sons of God came|Quadam die, quum venissent filii Dei]], that is, the holy angels, guardians of souls, came from those very men about whom they had been at work, and with whom they had really been present. For angels are in a place definitively [that is, wholly where they act and nowhere else, without being measured by the place as a body is], and where they work, there they are said to be; and when the ministry for which they came down is fulfilled, they soon return to heavenly things. For hence Daniel says: [[Dan 9:21|As I was yet speaking in prayer|Adhuc me loquente in oratione mea]], behold Gabriel [[Dan 9:21|flying swiftly, touched me|cito volans tetigit me]], and [[Dan 9:22|he instructed me|docuit me]]. And Gabriel said: [[Dan 9:22|I am now come forth to teach thee, and that thou mightest understand|Nunc egressus sum ut docerem te et intelligeres]]. [[Dan 9:23|I am come to shew it to thee|Ego autem veni ut indicarem tibi]]. So too we have in the book of Judges: [[Judg 2:1|an angel of the Lord went up from Galgal to the place of weepers|Angelus Domini ascendit de Galgala ad locum Flentium]]. And again: [[Judg 13:20|when the flame from the altar went up towards heaven, the angel of the Lord ascended also in the same|Quum ascenderet flamma altaris in cœlum, angelus Domini pariter in flamma ascendit]]. Moreover, the angel Raphael says to Tobias: [[Tob 12:20|It is time therefore that I return to him that sent me|Tempus est ut revertar ad eum qui me misit]]. And Zacharias the prophet bears witness: [[Zach 2:3|behold the angel that spoke in me went forth, and another angel went out to meet him|Ecce angelus qui loquebatur in me, egrediebatur, et alius angelus egrediebatur in occursum ejus]], and he said: [[Zach 2:4|Run, speak to this young man|Curre, et loquere ad puerum istum]]. From all these and many other places of Scripture it is plain that the holy angels are moved from place to place, and come from heaven to men, and return to heaven at hours and times foreordained by God.

paras.t: Ut adsisterent coram Domino. Si angeli indesinenter Deo adsistunt, utpote quem incessabiliter contemplantur, et a quo ipsi indeficienter cernuntur, quomodo quadam die venerunt ut coram Deo adsisterent? Et respondendum, quod semper adsistunt, quoad hoc quod jugiter cernunt atque cernuntur; nec hoc modo venerunt ut adsisterent. Sed angeli qui mittuntur, non solum dicuntur adsistere modo prædicto, verum etiam quoniam specialem aliquem actum de novo exhibent coram Deo. Propter quod dicit Albertus: Adsistunt, quum intima contemplatione vultui Dei præsentes sunt, et profectum ministerii sui ostendunt, et quid acturi sunt, per illuminationem a Deo accipiunt. Et illud, Quum venissent filii Dei, quidam exponunt sic: Ad præsentandum Deo merita hominum, prout in Tobiæ historia scribitur, quod preces Saræ et Tobiæ uno tempore in conspectu Dei sunt recitatæ. Et rursus ibidem Raphael fatetur Tobiæ: Quum orabas cum lacrimis et sepeliebas mortuos, ego obtuli orationem tuam Domino. Angeli equidem orationes et causas sibi commissorum ad divinum referunt judicium, suffragiumque impendunt. Unde Gabriel loquitur Danieli: Nunc revertar ut prælier adversus principem Persarum. Et ecce Michael unus de principibus primis venit in adjutorium meum. Sic ergo venerunt ut adsisterent coram Domino, per modum recentem ac specialem, ad peragendum actum præfatum.
paras.en: [[1:6|to stand before the Lord|Ut adsisterent coram Domino]]. If the angels stand before God unceasingly, since they contemplate Him without ceasing and are themselves seen by Him without fail, how did they come on a certain day to stand before God? The answer is that they always stand before Him, in that they continually see and are seen; and it was not in this way that they came to stand before Him. But the angels who are sent are said to stand before Him not only in the way just mentioned, but also because they perform before God some special act anew. Hence Albert says: They stand before Him when they are present to the face of God in inmost contemplation, and show the progress of their ministry, and receive from God by illumination what they are to do. And the words [[1:6|when the sons of God came|Quum venissent filii Dei]] some explain thus: to present to God the merits of men, as is written in the story of Tobias, that the prayers of Sara and of Tobias were rehearsed at one time in the sight of God[[Tob 3:25||]]. And again in the same place Raphael declares to Tobias: [[Tob 12:12|When thou didst pray with tears, and didst bury the dead|Quum orabas cum lacrimis et sepeliebas mortuos]], [[Tob 12:12|I offered thy prayer to the Lord|ego obtuli orationem tuam Domino]]. For the angels refer the prayers and the causes of those entrusted to them to God's judgment, and lend them their support. Hence Gabriel says to Daniel: [[Dan 10:20|now I will return, to fight against the prince of the Persians|Nunc revertar ut prælier adversus principem Persarum]]. And [[Dan 10:13|behold Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me|ecce Michael unus de principibus primis venit in adjutorium meum]]. So, then, they came [[1:6|to stand before the Lord|ut adsisterent coram Domino]] in a new and special manner, to perform the act mentioned above.

paras.t: Præterea alius modus est secundum quem angeli dicuntur a Deo exire, et ad ipsum venire atque redire ut ei adsistant: non quod a Deo ubique præsente usquam elongentur, avertantur, aut ejus beatifica visione priventur, quem non corporaliter extra se, sed spiritualiter intra se inavertibiliter contuentur; sed quia egrediuntur de loco, et regrediuntur ad locum illum, in quo Deus incircumscriptibilis et immensus specialiter esse habitareque dicitur: qui locus est cœlum empyreum, in quo Deus clarius se ostendit, et magnificentius agit. Sicque Raphael dixit: Tempus est ut revertar ad eum qui me misit. Et nihilo minus quando hoc dixit, etiam ait: Ego sum Raphael, unus de septem qui adstamus ante Deum. Ergo et tunc quando loquebatur Tobiæ in domo ejus, adstitit coram Deo. Habendo enim comparationem ad Deum secundum se, ubique ei præsentes sunt, nec redeunt ut adsistant: sed loquendo de Deo per comparationem ejus ad cœlum empyreum, in quo ipse specialiter esse et habitare asseritur, revertuntur ad ipsum, ut ei illic adsistant. Hinc dicit Gregorius: Et mittuntur igitur, et adsistunt: quia per hoc quod circumscripti sunt, exeunt; et per hoc quod intus præsentes sunt, nunquam recedunt. Et faciem ergo Patris semper vident, et tamen ad nos veniunt: quia et ad nos spirituali præsentia foras exeunt, et tamen unde recesserant, ibi se per internam contemplationem servant. Dicatur ergo, Venerunt filii Dei ut adsisterent coram Domino: quia illuc spiritus conversione redeunt, unde nulla mentis aversione discedunt.
paras.en: There is, besides, another way in which angels are said to go out from God, and to come and return to Him to stand before Him: not that they ever withdraw any distance from God, who is present everywhere, or turn away from Him, or are deprived of His beatific vision, for they behold Him without ever turning away, not bodily outside themselves but spiritually within themselves; but because they go out from, and go back to, that place in which God, who cannot be circumscribed and is immense, is said in a special way to be and to dwell: and that place is the empyrean heaven, in which God shows Himself more clearly and acts more magnificently. So Raphael said: [[Tob 12:20|It is time therefore that I return to him that sent me|Tempus est ut revertar ad eum qui me misit]]. And yet when he said this, he also said: [[Tob 12:15|I am the angel Raphael, one of the seven, who stand before the Lord|Ego sum Raphael, unus de septem qui adstamus ante Deum]]. Therefore even then, when he was speaking to Tobias in his house, he stood before God. For taking them in relation to God as He is in Himself, they are present to Him everywhere, and do not go back in order to stand before Him: but speaking of God in relation to the empyrean heaven, in which He is declared to be and to dwell in a special way, they return to Him so as to stand before Him there. Hence Gregory says: They are therefore both sent and stand before Him: for in that they are circumscribed, they go out; and in that they are present within, they never withdraw. So they both always see the face of the Father and yet come to us: for they go out to us by a spiritual presence, and yet keep themselves by inward contemplation there whence they had withdrawn. Let it be said, then, that [[1:6|the sons of God came to stand before the Lord|Venerunt filii Dei ut adsisterent coram Domino]]: for they return thither by the turning of the spirit, whence they never depart by any turning away of the mind.

paras.t: Postremo, angeli sancti dicuntur filii Dei ob eminentem similitudinem, qua per dona naturæ et gratiæ ei præclarius assimilantur. Dicit quoque Gregorius: Quia beati Job tentatio ad victoriam venit, a die cœpta perhibetur. Albertus quoque: Ideo, inquit, scriptum est, Quadam die, etc., quia in tantis doloribus et adversis a rationis et gratiæ luce non cecidit, et a tenebris ad lucem rediturus fuit, juxta illud Michææ: Ne lætaris, inimica mea, super me, quia cecidi: consurgam; quum sedero in tenebris, Dominus lux mea est.
paras.en: Lastly, the holy angels are called [[1:6|sons of God|filii Dei]] because of the eminent likeness by which, through the gifts of nature and of grace, they are made more splendidly like Him. Gregory also says: Because blessed Job's temptation came to victory, it is said to have been begun by day. And Albert: Therefore, he says, it is written, [[1:6|on a certain day|Quadam die]], etc., because amid such great sorrows and adversities he did not fall from the light of reason and of grace, and was to return from darkness to light, according to that of Micheas: [[Mich 7:8|Rejoice not, thou my enemy, over me, because I am fallen: I shall arise, when I sit in darkness, the Lord is my light|Ne lætaris, inimica mea, super me, quia cecidi: consurgam; quum sedero in tenebris, Dominus lux mea est]].

paras.t: Adfuit inter eos etiam Satan, est diabolus: non quod cœlum empyreum cum angelis sanctis ingrediatur, et ibi Deo adsistat; sed inter angelos adfuisse describitur multiplici ratione. Primo, quoniam angelis sanctis hominum merita Deo offerentibus, opemque quærentibus ac impendentibus, diabolus demerita hominum allegare, accusare, et salutem eorum impedire conatur, sicut super Danielem scribit Hieronymus: sicque inter eos est, intromittendo se de factis eorum. Secundo, propter communionem naturæ. Propter quod ait Gregorius: Recte inter eos fuisse describitur, quia etsi beatitudinem perdidit, naturam cum eis similem non amisit; etsi meritis prægravatur, conditione tamen naturæ subtilis attollitur. Tertio, quoniam sicut angelorum, ita et dæmonum natura ac operatio divino patent conspectui, ejusque adducuntur examini. Ideo dicit Albertus: Adfuit, quia divino lumini abscondere se nequivit. Quarto, secundum Thomam, dicitur adfuisse, ad insinuandum quod mala non sunt ex principali intentione, sed subveniunt bonis quasi per accidens. Quinto, quia eidem Domino cui angeli adstiterunt, præsens fuit et ipse.
paras.en: [[1:6|Satan also was present among them|Adfuit inter eos etiam Satan]], that is, the devil [the print has *est diabolus*, no doubt for *id est diabolus*]: not that he enters the empyrean heaven with the holy angels and stands before God there; but he is described as having been present among the angels for several reasons. First, because, while the holy angels offer men's merits to God, and seek and bestow help, the devil tries to allege men's demerits, to accuse them and to hinder their salvation, as Jerome writes on Daniel: and so he is among them by meddling in their doings. Secondly, because of their common nature. Hence Gregory says: He is rightly described as having been among them, because, though he lost beatitude, he did not lose a nature like theirs; though he is weighed down by his deserts, yet he is lifted up by the condition of a subtle nature. Thirdly, because, as the nature and working of the angels, so also those of the demons lie open to God's sight, and are brought to His examination. Therefore Albert says: He was present, because he could not hide himself from the divine light. Fourthly, according to Thomas, he is said to have been present to suggest that evils are not from the principal intention, but come in upon good things as it were by accident [*per accidens*: incidentally, not intended for their own sake]. Fifthly, because he too was present to the same Lord before whom the angels stood.

paras.t: Insuper Thomas dicit: Angeli venisse dicuntur, quia proprio motu et intentione omnia quæ agunt, divino subdunt judicio, referuntque in Deum. Mali vero angeli non intendunt quæ agunt referre in Deum, sed nolentibus eis hoc accidit, ut quidquid agant, divino subdatur judicio. Ideo non dicitur de Satan, quod venit ut adsisteret coram Domino, sed solum quod adfuit inter eos. Cui concordans Albertus, disseruit: Non dicit Scriptura quod venit vel vocatus fuit, sed adfuit, quasi coactus. Quibus obviare videtur, quod dæmones expetunt homines ad tentandum a Deo, et ex proposito sistunt se Deo ad accusandum; reos quoque quos ad supplicia trahere nequeunt, nisi prævio judicio Dei, sponte sequuntur vel ducunt ad judicem Christum, secundum modum Deo cognitum quo id fit. Hinc doctores præfati loqui videntur, quoad hoc quod dæmones quæ agunt, in Deum non referunt sicut ad finem, nec agunt quid ex proposito ad gloriam ejus directe; ea quoque quæ agunt, eis invitis, subduntur Dei judicio, in quantum hoc redundat in augmentum pœnæ eorum.
paras.en: Moreover Thomas says: The angels are said to have come because by their own motion and intention they submit all that they do to God's judgment, and refer it to God. But the bad angels do not intend to refer what they do to God; rather it befalls them against their will that whatever they do is subject to God's judgment. Therefore it is not said of Satan that he came to stand before the Lord, but only that he [[1:6|was present among them|adfuit inter eos]]. In agreement with this Albert discoursed: Scripture does not say that he came or was called, but that he was present, as if compelled. Against these it seems to tell that the demons ask God for men to tempt, and of set purpose present themselves before God to accuse them[[Apoc 12:10||]]; and the guilty too, whom they cannot drag to punishment except by God's previous judgment, they follow of their own accord or lead to Christ the judge, in a way known to God by which this is done. The doctors named, then, seem to be speaking with regard to this: that the demons do not refer what they do to God as to an end, nor do anything of set purpose directly for His glory; and that what they do is, against their will, subject to the judgment of God, inasmuch as this redounds to the increase of their punishment.

paras.t: Rursus ait Albertus: Dicit Scriptura quod Satan inter eos fuit, et non cum eis, vel ante eos, vel post eos. Cum eis non fuit, quia voluntati eorum non concordavit; ante eos non fuit, quia profectus eorum in bonis hominibus impedire non potuit; post eos non fuit, quoniam confirmatis insidiari non potuit; sed inter eos fuit, quum inter bona eorum mala seminavit, juxta illud Matthæi: Quum dormirent homines, venit inimicus, et superseminavit zizania in medio tritici. Id etiam advertendum, quod angeli sancti cum hominibus in terra consistendo, preces eorum ac merita Deo possunt offerre ac opem impendere, atque ibidem se sistere Domino secundum modum prætactum, sicque venire ad ipsum, convertendo se de actu circa hominem exhibito, ad actum circa Deum versantem, qui est præsentare merita hominum Deo, non quasi Deus ea ignoret, sed ut optatum ab ipso sortiantur gratiæ donum: sicque inter eos Satan adesset.
paras.en: Again Albert says: Scripture says that Satan was among them, and not with them, or before them, or after them. He was not with them, because he did not agree with their will; he was not before them, because he could not hinder their progress in good men; he was not after them, because he could not lie in wait for those confirmed in grace; but he was among them, in that he sowed evil among their good things, according to that of Matthew: [[Matt 13:25|while men were asleep|Quum dormirent homines]], the enemy came, [[Matt 13:25|and oversowed cockle among the wheat|et superseminavit zizania in medio tritici]]. This too is to be noted: that the holy angels, while staying with men on earth, can offer their prayers and merits to God and bestow help, and there present themselves to the Lord in the way touched on above, and so come to Him, turning from the act shown towards man to the act directed towards God, which is to present men's merits to God, not as if God did not know them, but that they may obtain from Him the gift of grace desired: and in this way Satan might be among them.

paras.t: Cui dixit Dominus, allocutione non exteriore, corporali, sensibili, sed interiore ac intelligibili, quum ipsemet Deus sit supersimplicissimus spiritus, dæmon quoque spiritualis substantia est: Unde venis? Quærendum cur angelis bonis Deus non ait, Unde venitis? sed Satanæ, Unde venis? Ad quod respondet Gregorius: Requirimus quæ nescimus; nescire autem Dei, est reprobare: unde quibusdam dicturum se perhibet, Nescio vos unde sitis. Sic verax homo dicitur nescire mentiri, quia fari mendacium dedignatur. Quoniam ergo Dominus Satanæ vias reprobat, ait ad eum: Unde venis? Et est quæstio non ignorantis, sed arguentis: tanquam dicat, Vide de quantis obscœnitatibus atque malitiis venias. Similiter dicitur Adæ: Adam, ubi es? id est, vide in quanta miseria es. Locutio quoque ista perficitur, dum Satanæ sua malitia divino lumine demonstratur, ut dicit Albertus.
paras.en: [[1:7|And the Lord said to him|Cui dixit Dominus]], by an address not exterior, bodily and sensible, but interior and intelligible, since God Himself is a spirit simple beyond all simplicity, and the demon too is a spiritual substance: [[1:7|Whence comest thou?|Unde venis?]] It is to be asked why God did not say to the good angels, Whence come you? but to Satan, [[1:7|Whence comest thou?|Unde venis?]] To which Gregory answers: We inquire about what we do not know; but for God not to know is to reject [*reprobare*: to disown, condemn]: hence He declares that He will say to some, [[Luke 13:25|I know you not, whence you are|Nescio vos unde sitis]][[Matt 25:12||]]. So a truthful man is said not to know how to lie, because he disdains to utter a lie. Since, then, the Lord rejects the ways of Satan, He says to him: [[1:7|Whence comest thou?|Unde venis?]] And it is the question not of one who does not know, but of one who rebukes: as if He said, See from what great obscenities and wickednesses thou comest. In the same way it is said to Adam: Adam, [[Gen 3:9|Where art thou?|ubi es?]] that is, see in how great a misery thou art. This speech, too, is accomplished when Satan's wickedness is shown to him by the divine light, as Albert says.

paras.t: Thomas autem hanc quæstionem solvit, dicendo: Angeli boni nil faciunt, nisi ad quod divina voluntate moventur: a qua angeli mali discordant; unde quæ agunt, a Deo aliena exsistunt, quantum ad intentionem eorum semper perversam. Non autem solemus interrogare de his quæ ipsi nos facimus, sed de his quæ absque nobis fiunt: ideo non dicitur quod Dominus interrogavit ab angelis bonis, sed solum a Satan. Potest insuper responderi, quod ideo, quoniam angeli boni bene sibi conscii, ad hoc coram Deo adstiterunt, ut ei sua opera faterentur ac præsentarent per modum prædictum: ideo non inquiruntur. Satan vero male sibi conscius, ita non habuit se; imo quantum in se est, suam mallet occultare nequitiam, in quantum est sua: hinc interrogatur. Quem etiam Dominus idcirco non quasi ignorans interrogat, ut ejus responsione convenienter procedat ad quod intendebat, scilicet ad sancti Job commendationem.
paras.en: Thomas, however, solves this question by saying: The good angels do nothing but that to which they are moved by the divine will; and from it the bad angels are at variance; hence what they do is alien to God, as regards their intention, which is always perverse. Now we are not accustomed to ask about the things which we ourselves do, but about those which are done without us: therefore it is not said that the Lord questioned the good angels, but only Satan. It can also be answered that, since the good angels, having a good conscience, stood before God for this purpose, that they might confess their works to Him and present them in the way described, they are therefore not questioned. But Satan, having an evil conscience, did not behave so; rather, as far as in him lay, he would prefer to hide his wickedness, inasmuch as it is his own: hence he is questioned. And the Lord questions him, not as one who does not know, for this reason: that by his answer He may fittingly proceed to what He intended, namely the commendation of holy Job.

paras.t: Insuper, juxta Thomam, Dominus non ait ad Satan, Quid facis? aut, Ubi es? sed, Unde venis? Quoniam facta quæ per dæmones procurantur, interdum ex divina voluntate procedunt, dum per eos vel mali puniuntur, vel boni exercentur; sed dæmonis intentio semper est mala, atque a Domino aliena. Iterum, secundum eumdem Doctorem, dicere, dupliciter accipitur: quandoque enim refertur ad cordis conceptum, quandoque ad significationem, qua talis conceptus exprimitur alteri. Itaque secundum primum modum, dicere Dei æternum est, nihilque aliud quam generare Filium, qui est Verbum ipsius. Secundo modo dicit specialiter aliqua Deus, diversimode tamen diversis, secundum quod congruit naturæ eorum. Hominibus quippe corporeos sensus habentibus quandoque locutus est sono sensibili, formato in aliqua creatura subjecta, sicut vox sonuit in baptismo transfigurationeque Christi, Hic est Filius meus dilectus. Aliquando per visionem imaginariam, ut Prophetis. Aliquando autem intelligibili expressione: sicque intelligendum est, Deum ad Satan dixisse, in quantum Deus fecit ipsum Satan intelligere, quod ea quæ agit, conspiciuntur a Deo. Sicut autem dicere Dei ad Satan, est notitiam ei præbere; sic Satan Deo respondere, est non alicujus rei notitiam Deo tradere, sed considerare omnia Dei conspectui aperta esse.
paras.en: Moreover, according to Thomas, the Lord does not say to Satan, What doest thou? or, Where art thou? but, [[1:7|Whence comest thou?|Unde venis?]] Because the deeds brought about through the demons sometimes proceed from the divine will, when through them either the wicked are punished or the good are exercised; but the demon's intention is always evil, and alien to the Lord. Again, according to the same Doctor, *to say* is taken in two ways: for sometimes it refers to the conception of the heart, sometimes to the signifying by which such a conception is expressed to another. So in the first way God's saying is eternal, and is nothing other than to beget the Son, who is His Word. In the second way God says certain things in particular, yet differently to different beings, according as befits their nature. For to men, who have bodily senses, He has sometimes spoken by a sensible sound formed in some subject creature, as the voice sounded at the baptism and the transfiguration of Christ: [[Matt 3:17|This is my beloved Son|Hic est Filius meus dilectus]][[Matt 17:5||]]. Sometimes by an imaginary vision [that is, one formed in the imagination, not a fancy], as to the Prophets. But sometimes by an intelligible expression: and so it is to be understood that God spoke to Satan, inasmuch as God made Satan himself understand that the things he does are beheld by God. And as God's saying to Satan is to give him knowledge, so Satan's answering God is not to impart to God the knowledge of anything, but to consider that all things are open to God's sight[[Heb 4:13||]] [the margin gives Hebr. iii, 15, which does not fit; the words echo Heb 4:13].

paras.t: Verumtamen de hoc plenius tractat Gregorius, dicens: Quatuor modis loquitur Deus diabolo. Primo, vias ejus injustas arguendo, sicut dum ait: Unde venis? Secundo, electorum justitiam contra eum proponendo, ut quum dicit: Numquid considerasti servum meum Job, quod non sit ei similis super terram? Tertio, tentandam electorum innocentiam dæmoni permittendo, quemadmodum ait: Ecce universa quæ habet, in manu tua sunt. Quarto, diabolum ab electorum tentatione aliquando prohibendo, sicut subjungit: Tantum in eum ne extendas manum tuam. Quæ omnia loquendi genera fiunt per intelligibilem ostensionem. Tribus quoque modis diabolus loquitur Domino. Primo, vias suas ei denuntiando, ut quum ait: Circuivi terram, etc. Secundo, electos mendaciter accusando, sicut quum dicit: Numquid frustra Job timet Deum? Tertio, tentandam eorum innocentiam postulando, ut quum ait: Extende manum tuam, et tange cuncta quæ possidet, etc.
paras.en: However, Gregory treats of this more fully, saying: In four ways God speaks to the devil. First, by reproving his unjust ways, as when He says: [[1:7|Whence comest thou?|Unde venis?]] Secondly, by setting the justice of the elect against him, as when He says: [[1:8|Hast thou considered my servant, Job, that there is none like him in the earth|Numquid considerasti servum meum Job, quod non sit ei similis super terram?]]? Thirdly, by permitting the demon to try the innocence of the elect, as when He says: [[1:12|Behold, all that he hath is in thy hand|Ecce universa quæ habet, in manu tua sunt]]. Fourthly, by sometimes forbidding the devil to tempt the elect, as He adds: [[1:12|only put not forth thy hand upon his person|Tantum in eum ne extendas manum tuam]]. All these kinds of speaking take place by an intelligible showing. In three ways, too, the devil speaks to the Lord. First, by declaring his ways to Him, as when he says: [[1:7|I have gone round about the earth|Circuivi terram]], etc. Secondly, by falsely accusing the elect, as when he says: [[1:9|Doth Job fear God in vain?|Numquid frustra Job timet Deum?]] Thirdly, by asking that their innocence be tried, as when he says: [[1:11|stretch forth thy hand|Extende manum tuam]], [[1:11|and touch all that he hath|et tange cuncta quæ possidet]], etc.

paras.t: Adhuc secundum Albertum, isti modi locutionum fiunt per demonstrationes illuminationum, id est ostensivas illuminationes, quantum videlicet ad superiores. Demonstrationem autem illuminationum appellat, quando ex voluntate intellectualis substantia in lumine intelligentiæ suæ conceptus suos atque affectus alteri substantiæ intellectuali demonstrat. Et hoc dicit Basilius in libro de Fide divinitatis sic: Sermonis usum nobis Deus inclusit, ut corporei exsistentes, affectus nostros invicem panderemus. Si autem intecta et nuda anima uteremur, sermone non indigeremus, sed mutuo in nobis invicem videremus nostros affectus. Hinc quoque Gregorius ait: Alienis oculis intra mentis nostræ secretum, quasi post parietem corporis stamus; sed quum manifestare nos ipsos cupimus, quasi per linguæ januam egredimur.
paras.en: Further, according to Albert, these modes of speech take place by demonstrations of illuminations, that is, by illuminations that show something, at least as regards the higher spirits. He calls it a demonstration of illuminations when an intellectual substance, by its will, shows its conceptions and affections to another intellectual substance in the light of its understanding. And Basil says this in the book On the Faith of the Godhead, thus: God has implanted in us the use of speech, so that, being bodily, we might lay open our affections to one another. But if we had a soul uncovered and bare, we should not need speech, but should see our affections mutually in one another. Hence Gregory too says: To the eyes of others we stand within the secret place of our mind as if behind the wall of the body; but when we wish to make ourselves known, we go out as if through the door of the tongue.

paras.t: Qui respondens ait. Jam dictum est, quid sit, et quomodo fiat responsio Satan ad Deum: fatetur equidem Deo quod ei abscondere nequit, imo quod ille invariabiliter præscit. Circuivi terram, id est habitatores terræ, et perambulavi eam, id est, diligenter pertransivi. Omnium enim mores, proprietates, inclinationes, consuetudines, actus, vitamque observat, ventilat, discutit atque rimatur, ut sciat qualiter quemque facilius vincat, astutius tentet, secretius circumveniat, damnabiliusque prosternat. Unde per circuitum ejus calliditas designatur, curvitas sive perversitas, sicut per rectitudinem simplicitas atque justitia. Callidorum namque est aliud foris prætendere, aliud intus intendere, et sic opus quod faciunt ac ostendunt, exit ab extremis, dum neque voluntati concordat, nec ultimo fini. Rursus, dæmon et homines vitiosi mente semper instabiles sunt et undique divagantur, quia in Deo summo et incommutabili bono mentis non figunt radicem. Ideo scriptum est: In circuitu impii ambulant. Et in prima Petri: Sobrii estote et vigilate, quia adversarius vester diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret.
paras.en: [[1:7|And he answered and said|Qui respondens ait]]. It has already been said what Satan's answer to God is, and how it takes place: for he confesses to God what he cannot hide from Him, indeed what He unchangeably foreknows. [[1:7|I have gone round about the earth|Circuivi terram]], that is, the inhabitants of the earth, [[1:7|and walked through it|et perambulavi eam]], that is, I have gone through it carefully. For he observes, sifts, examines and searches into the manners, properties, inclinations, habits, acts and life of all, so as to know how he may most easily overcome each one, most craftily tempt him, most secretly ensnare him, and most damnably lay him low. Hence by his going round is signified craftiness, crookedness or perversity, as by straightness are signified simplicity and justice. For it belongs to the crafty to put forward one thing outwardly and to intend another inwardly; and so the work which they do and show comes forth from the outer edges [that is, as from the circumference and not from the centre, keeping the image of going round], since it agrees neither with their will nor with the last end. Again, the demon and vicious men are always unstable in mind and wander about on all sides, because they do not fix the root of the mind in God, the highest and unchangeable good. Therefore it is written: [[Ps 11:9|The wicked walk round about|In circuitu impii ambulant]]. And in the first Epistle of Peter: [[1 Pet 5:8|Be sober and watch: because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour|Sobrii estote et vigilate, quia adversarius vester diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret]].

paras.t: Dicit autem Albertus: Perambulat, qui ubique vestigium pedis relinquit; vestigium vero pedis diaboli, peccatum est. Sed sic non perambulat, nisi quos aliquo modo vincit atque contaminat. Virtuosi autem eum expellunt, implentes illud Apostoli, Nolite locum dare diabolo; imo de ejus impugnatione triumphando, puriores redduntur.
paras.en: Albert, moreover, says: He *walks through* who leaves the print of his foot everywhere; and the footprint of the devil is sin. But he does not walk through in this way any but those whom he in some way overcomes and defiles. The virtuous, however, drive him out, fulfilling that saying of the Apostle, [[Eph 4:27|Give not place to the devil|Nolite locum dare diabolo]]; rather, by triumphing over his assault, they are made purer.

1.t: Vir erat in terra Hus, nomine Job. Primo historia quædam inducitur, quæ totius sequentis disputationis velut fundamentum et thema est, ad declarandum qualiter actus hominum providentia gubernentur divina. Porro de persona, nomine, cognatione et terra Job, dicta sunt plurima primo articulo: unde ex dictis ibidem patet intelligentia hujus particulæ textus. Fuit autem Job vir triplici virilitatis perfectione, videlicet perfectione animi per virtutum constantiam, perfectione naturæ per virentem germinationem, perfectione sexus. Sexus namque masculinus perfectior est, et ad sustinendas molestias fortior: ideo decuit personam, in qua patientiæ exemplum præclarum fuerat demonstrandum, esse sexus virilis. Denique secundum Gregorium, perfectione animi vir vocatur, qui contra biformes fortunæ insultus uniformi mentis constantia militat: qui scilicet nec prosperis vane extollitur, nec adversis mente dejicitur, sed regia via semper incedit. Hinc ad Eugenium Papam ait Bernardus: Magnus est cui dignitas sæculi si arrisit, non irrisit; nec minor est illo, qui incidens in adversa, non excidit a sapientia. Quam perfectionem adepta est sancta Anna, de qua primo Regum habetur, Vultus ejus non sunt amplius in diversa mutati; et beatissimus pater noster S. Martinus, de quo testatur Severus, quod nemo illum unquam vidit tristem aut dissolutum. Itaque et nos conemur taliter viri esse: quod erit, si passiones fuerint reformatæ, omnesque animarum nostrarum affectiones in Deum stabiliter ordinatæ.
1.en: [[1:1|There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job|Vir erat in terra Hus, nomine Job]]. First a certain history is set down, which is as it were the foundation and theme of the whole disputation that follows, to make plain how the acts of men are governed by divine providence. Of the person, name, kindred and land of Job a great deal was said in the first article, so the meaning of this little part of the text is clear from what was said there. Now Job was a man with a threefold perfection of manhood: perfection of soul through constancy in the virtues, perfection of nature through flourishing fruitfulness, and perfection of sex [Denis plays on *vir*, “man”, *virilitas*, “manhood”, *virtus*, “virtue”, and *virens*, “flourishing”]. For the male sex is the more perfect, and the stronger for bearing hardships; and so it was fitting that the person in whom a shining example of patience was to be shown should be of the male sex. Further, according to Gregory, he is called a man (*vir*) for perfection of soul who fights against the twofold assaults of fortune with an unchanging constancy of mind: that is, who is neither vainly lifted up by prosperity nor cast down in mind by adversity, but always walks the royal road. Hence Bernard says to Pope Eugene: Great is he on whom the dignity of the world has smiled without mocking him [*arrisit, non irrisit*, a play on “smiled on” and “laughed at”]; nor is he less who, falling into adversity, has not fallen away from wisdom. This perfection holy Anna attained, of whom it is said in the First Book of Kings: [[1 Kings 1:18|her countenance was no more changed|Vultus ejus non sunt amplius in diversa mutati]]; and our most blessed father St Martin, of whom Severus testifies that no one ever saw him sad or unbridled. Let us too, then, strive to be men in this way: and so we shall be, if our passions have been reformed and all the affections of our souls steadily ordered towards God.

1.t: Præterea secundum Gregorium, terra in qua Job habitavit, exprimitur, ut ex hoc perfectio suæ virtutis amplius commendetur. Hus namque est terra gentilium: sicque dum scribitur inter malos fuisse moratus, perfectior declaratur. Item Gregorius: Neque enim valde laudabile est, bonum esse cum bonis, sed bonum esse cum malis. Quemadmodum autem gravioris est culpæ, inter bonos bonum non esse; ita immensi præconii est, etiam inter malos bonum consistere.
1.en: Moreover, according to Gregory, the land in which Job dwelt is named so that the perfection of his virtue may be the more commended by it. For Hus is a land of the Gentiles; and so, when it is written that he lived among the wicked, he is shown to be the more perfect. Gregory again: For it is not very praiseworthy to be good with the good, but to be good with the wicked. For as it is the graver fault not to be good among the good, so it is a matter of immense praise to stand good even among the wicked.

1.t: Et erat vir ille simplex, triplici simplicitate, secundum Albertum (per quem in toto hoc opere intelligo Albertum Magnum ordinis Prædicatorum), videlicet simplicitate intentionis: quoniam in omnibus quæ agebat, unum summum bonum intendebat. De qua simplicitate loquitur Christus, Si oculus tuus fuerit simplex, totum corpus tuum lucidum erit: cui simplicitati opponitur duplicitas cordis volentium Deo et mundo placere, nuncque gaudere cum sæculo, et postea regnare cum Christo; cum tamen ipse testatus sit: Nemo potest duobus dominis servire. Unde Ecclesiasticus quoque asserit: Væ peccatori ingredienti terram duabus viis. Et iterum: Ne accesseris ad Deum duplici corde. Quantum hæc bona simplicitas placeat Deo, patet ex eo quod Salomon profitetur: Cum simplicibus sermocinatio ejus. Ad Philippenses quoque ait Apostolus: Sitis sine querela, simplices filii Dei. Secundo, fuit simplex simplicitate virtutis in generali: quæ simplicitas consistit in hoc, quod virtus est ex una sola totaque causa, secundum divinum Dionysium atque Philosophum, vitium vero ex causa multiplici. Huic simplicitati opponitur multiplicitas peccati, juxta illud secundi Paralipomenon: Peccavi super numerum arenæ maris; multiplicatæ sunt iniquitates meæ. Tertio, simplicitate prudentiæ, quæ est sine plica astutiæ, dolositatis et tergiversationis ad malum. Itaque accipitur hic simplicitas non ut opponitur intellectus perspicacitati, sed dolositati. Est namque et mala ac asinina simplicitas per debitæ considerationis defectum, ad quam pertinere potest illud Proverbiorum: Simplex credit omni verbo; astutus considerat gressus suos. Potestque ibi astutia sumi in bono.
1.en: [[1:1|and that man was simple|Et erat vir ille simplex]], with a threefold simplicity, according to Albert (by whom throughout this work I mean Albert the Great, of the Order of Preachers). First, by simplicity of intention, since in all that he did he intended the one supreme good. Of this simplicity Christ speaks: [[Matt 6:22|If thy eye be single, thy whole body shall be lightsome|Si oculus tuus fuerit simplex, totum corpus tuum lucidum erit]]. To this simplicity is opposed the doubleness of heart of those who wish to please God and the world, to rejoice with the world now and afterwards to reign with Christ; though he himself has testified: [[Matt 6:24|No man can serve two masters|Nemo potest duobus dominis servire]]. Hence Ecclesiasticus too declares: [[Ecclus 2:14|Woe|Væ]] [[Ecclus 2:14|to the sinner that goeth on the earth two ways|peccatori ingredienti terram duabus viis]]. And again: [[Ecclus 1:36|come not to him with a double heart|Ne accesseris ad Deum duplici corde]]. How much this good simplicity pleases God is clear from what Solomon professes: [[Prov 3:32|his communication is with the simple|Cum simplicibus sermocinatio ejus]]. The Apostle too says to the Philippians: [[Phil 2:15|That you may be blameless and sincere children of God|Sitis sine querela, simplices filii Dei]]. Secondly, he was simple with the simplicity of virtue in general: this simplicity consists in this, that virtue comes from one single and entire cause, according to the divine Dionysius and the Philosopher, but vice from a manifold cause [that is, an act is good only when everything in it is right, but evil from any one defect]. To this simplicity is opposed the multiplicity of sin, according to that word of the Second Book of Paralipomenon: I have sinned above the number of the sand of the sea; my iniquities are multiplied [these words are from the Prayer of Manasses, printed in the Vulgate after the Second Book of Paralipomenon; it is not in the Douay-Rheims text used in this app]. Thirdly, with the simplicity of prudence, which is without the fold of craft, deceit and shuffling towards evil [Denis takes *simplex*, “simple”, as *sine plica*, “without a fold”]. So simplicity is taken here not as it is opposed to keenness of understanding, but as it is opposed to deceitfulness. For there is also a bad and asinine simplicity, through lack of due consideration, to which that word of Proverbs may belong: [[Prov 14:15|The innocent believeth every word: the discreet man considereth his steps|Simplex credit omni verbo; astutus considerat gressus suos]] [Denis reads *simplex*, “the simple man”, where the Vulgate has *innocens*]. And there craftiness [*astutus*, “crafty”, which the Douay-Rheims renders “discreet”] may be taken in a good sense.

1.t: Fuit autem et rectus, id est justus affectu et opere. Rectitudo equidem proprie ad justitiam pertinet, quæ in æqualitate consistit, juxta illud Isaiæ: Semita justi recta est. Quocontra de impiis Salomon ait: Relinquunt iter rectum, et ambulant per vias tenebrosas. Porro recta itinera sunt divina præcepta, sine vitiorum obliquitate ad beatitudinem veram ducentia: per quæ justi pede ambulant inoffenso, pravi vero in eis labuntur, juxta illud Osee: Rectæ viæ Domini, et justi ambulabunt in eis; prævaricatores autem corruent in eis. Denique Ambrosius ait: Rectus est qui suam voluntatem conformat divinæ, volens de omni re quod Deus vult eum velle, et ex eadem caritate qua Deus, vult quod vult. Anselmus quoque: Justitia, inquit, est rectitudo sola mente perceptibilis. Ex quo certum est, quod rectitudo ad justitiam spectet. Itaque rectus est qui per lineas æquitatis in actibus suis procedit. Rectum namque est, ut etiam a Platone asseritur, cujus medium non exit ab extremis. Extrema vero operationis humanæ sunt: prima principia in operabilibus, sicut est illud Salvatoris in Evangelio, Quæcumque vultis ut faciant vobis homines, facite eis; et illud Tobiæ, Quod ab alio oderis fieri tibi, vide ne aliquando alii facias; et ultimus finis, puta æterna felicitas. Job ergo et omnis justus dicitur rectus, quoniam in actibus suis processit a principiis operabilium, absque declinatione ad culpam, ad ultimum finem.
1.en: He was also [[1:1|upright|rectus]], that is, just in affection and in deed. Uprightness [*rectitudo*, “rightness” or “straightness”] belongs properly to justice, which consists in equality, according to that word of Isaias: [[Is 26:7|The way of the just is right|Semita justi recta est]]. Whereas of the wicked Solomon says: [[Prov 2:13|leave the right way, and walk by dark ways|Relinquunt iter rectum, et ambulant per vias tenebrosas]]. Now the right roads are the divine precepts, which lead to true beatitude without the crookedness of vices: by them the just walk with unstumbling foot, while the wicked slip in them, according to that word of Osee: [[Osee 14:10|the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them: but the transgressors shall fall in them|Rectæ viæ Domini, et justi ambulabunt in eis; prævaricatores autem corruent in eis]]. Ambrose, further, says: He is upright who conforms his own will to the divine, willing in every matter what God wills him to will, and willing what he wills out of the same charity as God. Anselm too: Justice, he says, is rightness perceptible to the mind alone. From this it is certain that uprightness concerns justice. And so he is upright who goes forward in his acts along the lines of equity. For the straight [*rectum*, the same word as “upright”], as Plato too asserts, is that whose middle does not stray from its extremes [that is, from the line between its two ends]. Now the extremes of human action are, first, the first principles in matters of action, such as that word of the Saviour in the Gospel: [[Matt 7:12|whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do you also to them|Quæcumque vultis ut faciant vobis homines, facite eis]]; and that of Tobias: [[Tob 4:16|See thou never do to another what thou wouldst hate to have done to thee by another|Quod ab alio oderis fieri tibi, vide ne aliquando alii facias]]; and, second, the last end, namely eternal happiness. Job therefore, and every just man, is called upright, since in his acts he went forward from the principles of action to the last end without turning aside to sin.

1.t: At vero secundum Gregorium, quidam ita sunt simplices, ut quid sit rectum, ignorent; sed eo veræ simplicitatis innocentiam deserunt, quo ad virtutem rectitudinis non assurgunt. Propter quod Paulus ait: Volo vos sapientes esse in bono, simplices autem in malo. Et ipsemet Christus: Estote prudentes sicut serpentes, et simplices sicut columbæ; ut scilicet simplicitatem columbæ astutia serpentis instrueret, et serpentis astutiam columbæ simplicitas temperaret. Hinc Spiritus Sanctus non in specie columbæ tantum, sed et in igne apparuit. Per columbam namque simplicitas, per ignem zelus exprimitur. Qui autem repleti sunt Spiritu Sancto, sic mansuetudini simplicitatis deserviunt, ut contra delinquentium culpas etiam zelo rectitudinis accendantur. Hinc et Salomon duo ista conjungit, dicens: Qui recti sunt, habitabunt in terra, et simplices permanebunt in ea.
1.en: But according to Gregory, some are so simple that they do not know what is right; and they forsake the innocence of true simplicity by the very fact that they do not rise to the virtue of uprightness. For this reason Paul says: [[Rom 16:19|I would have you to be wise in good and simple in evil|Volo vos sapientes esse in bono, simplices autem in malo]].
